knowledge_statements.statement_title: Forests, trees, and spanning-tree characterizations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Foundational definitions and structural facts for finite undirected graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A forest is a graph with no circuits, and a tree is a connected forest. If a forest (V,E) has \kappa components, then |E|=|V|-\kappa; hence a tree has |E|=|V|-1. Every forest having at least one edge has an end vertex, and a connected subgraph of a tree T is a subtree of T. For F\subseteq E(G), F is a forest when (V,F) is a forest and is a spanning tree when (V,F) is a tree. Moreover, G has a spanning tree if and only if G is connected. If G is connected, then F is a spanning tree if and only if F is an inclusionwise maximal forest, if and only if F is an inclusionwise minimal edge set such that (V,F) is connected.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Forests are acyclic graphs and trees are connected forests. A forest with κ components has |V|−κ edges, while a tree has |V|−1. A graph has a spanning tree exactly when it is connected; in a connected graph, spanning trees are exactly the maximal forests and the minimal connected spanning edge sets.
assumptions_latex: G=(V,E)\text{ is a finite undirected graph}
\kappa\text{ is the number of components of the relevant forest}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: |E|=|V|-\kappa;\quad G\text{ is connected}\Longleftrightarrow G\text{ has a spanning tree};\quad F\text{ is a spanning tree}\Longleftrightarrow F\text{ is an inclusionwise maximal forest}\Longleftrightarrow (V,F)\text{ is inclusionwise minimally connected}

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A tree is a connected undirected graph with no cycles, and a leaf is a node of the tree having degree one.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: G\text{ is a tree}\iff G\text{ is connected and acyclic};\qquad v\text{ is a leaf}\iff \deg_G(v)=1.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Extension of an acyclic edge set to a spanning tree
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States the spanning-tree extension property for an acyclic edge subset of a connected undirected graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(\mathcal N,\mathcal E)\) be a connected undirected graph, and let \(\mathcal E_0\subseteq\mathcal E\) contain no cycle. Then there exists \(\mathcal E_1\) satisfying \(\mathcal E_0\subseteq\mathcal E_1\subseteq\mathcal E\) such that \((\mathcal N,\mathcal E_1)\) is a spanning tree of \(G\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every acyclic subset of the edges of a connected undirected graph can be extended, using edges of that graph, to a spanning tree.
assumptions_latex: G=(\mathcal N,\mathcal E)\text{ is a connected undirected graph}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists\mathcal E_1:\ \mathcal E_0\subseteq\mathcal E_1\subseteq\mathcal E\ \land\ (\mathcal N,\mathcal E_1)\text{ is a spanning tree of }G.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Trees, Forests, and Spanning Trees in an Ambient Graph
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Tree and forest subgraphs of an undirected graph, including maximal forests in the connected case.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A tree in $G$ is a connected acyclic subgraph of $G$. A forest in $G$ is an acyclic subgraph of $G$; equivalently, each component of the forest is a tree. If $G$ is connected, then every inclusion-maximal forest in $G$ is a spanning tree of $G$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A tree in a graph is a connected acyclic subgraph, while a forest is an acyclic subgraph whose components are trees. In a connected graph, every inclusion-maximal forest is a spanning tree.
assumptions_latex: G\text{ is connected for the maximal-forest conclusion.}
\text{Maximality is inclusion maximality among forests contained in }G.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: G\text{ connected and }F\subseteq G\text{ an inclusion-maximal forest}\implies F\text{ is a spanning tree of }G.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Elementary structural properties of finite trees
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Collects leaf existence, the connected edge-count characterization, unique paths, and the unique-cycle effect of adding an edge.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For finite simple undirected graphs: (a) every tree with more than one node has at least one leaf; (b) an undirected graph \(G=(\mathcal N,\mathcal E)\) is a tree if and only if it is connected and \(|\mathcal E|=|\mathcal N|-1\); (c) every two distinct nodes of a tree are joined by a unique path; and (d) if \(e\) is a new edge joining two distinct nodes of a tree \(T\), then \(T+e\) contains exactly one cycle, counted as an unoriented cyclic subgraph rather than by alternative traversal descriptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every finite tree with more than one node has a leaf. A finite undirected graph is a tree exactly when it is connected and has one fewer edge than nodes. Every two distinct tree nodes have a unique path between them, and adding a new edge between two tree nodes creates one cycle, without counting alternate descriptions of that same cycle separately.
assumptions_latex: G=(\mathcal N,\mathcal E)\text{ is a finite simple undirected graph}
T\text{ is a tree in the clauses concerning trees}
e=\{u,v\}\notin E(T),\quad u,v\in V(T),\quad u\ne v\text{ in clause (d)}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: |V(T)|>1\Rightarrow T\text{ has a leaf};\quad G\text{ is a tree}\iff G\text{ is connected and }|E(G)|=|V(G)|-1;\quad \forall i\ne j\in V(T),\ \exists!\text{ an }i\text{--}j\text{ path};\quad T+e\text{ contains exactly one cycle}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Trees, forests, and spanning trees
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definitions and elementary structural properties of finite undirected trees and forests.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A tree is a connected acyclic undirected graph. A forest is an acyclic undirected graph, and each connected component of a forest is a tree. For a finite undirected graph \(G=(N,E)\), any two of connectedness, acyclicity, and \(|E|=|N|-1\) imply the third. Every connected graph contains a spanning tree. If an edge \(e\notin T\) is added to a spanning tree \(T\), it creates a unique cycle \(C\); for every \(f\in C\), \(T+e-f\) is again a spanning tree.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A tree is a connected acyclic undirected graph, while a forest is an acyclic undirected graph whose connected components are trees. In a finite graph, any two of connectedness, acyclicity, and having one fewer edge than vertices imply the third. Every connected graph has a spanning tree. Adding a non-tree edge to a spanning tree creates one cycle, and removing any edge of that cycle again yields a spanning tree.
assumptions_latex: G=(N,E)\text{ is a finite undirected graph}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: G\text{ is a tree}\iff G\text{ is connected and acyclic};\quad |E|=|N|-1\text{ for every tree};\quad T+e-f\text{ is a spanning tree for }f\in C(T+e).

knowledge_statements.title: Spanning Trees
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard finite nonempty undirected-graph definition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite undirected graph with \(V\neq\varnothing\). A set \(T\subseteq E\) is a spanning tree of \(G\) if the spanning subgraph \((V,T)\) is connected and contains no cycle. Equivalently, \(T\) is a spanning tree if and only if \((V,T)\) is connected and \(|T|=|V|-1\), or if and only if it is acyclic and \(|T|=|V|-1\). Such a set exists exactly when \(G\) is connected.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a finite nonempty graph, a spanning tree is an acyclic connected subgraph containing every vertex; the graph has one exactly when it is connected.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite undirected graph with \(V\neq\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T\subseteq E\) is a spanning tree exactly when \((V,T)\) is connected and acyclic.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strongly polynomial convex decomposition of a spanning-tree-polytope point
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Constructive representation by incidence vectors of spanning trees.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every graph \(G=(V,E)\) and every \(y\in P_{\mathrm{spanning\ tree}}(G)\), one can find, in strongly polynomial time, spanning trees \(T_1,\ldots,T_k\) and coefficients \(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_k\ge 0\) such that \(\sum_{i=1}^k\lambda_i=1\) and \(y=\sum_{i=1}^k\lambda_i\chi^{T_i}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A point in the spanning-tree polytope can be decomposed in strongly polynomial time into a convex combination of spanning-tree incidence vectors.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{In strongly polynomial time, find spanning trees }T_1,\ldots,T_k\text{ and }\lambda_i\ge0\text{ such that }\sum_{i=1}^k\lambda_i=1\text{ and }y=\sum_{i=1}^k\lambda_i\chi^{T_i}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Single-arc exchange between spanning trees
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Basis exchange specialized to the spanning trees of a connected graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T_1\) and \(T_2\) be spanning trees of a connected graph \(G\). For every arc \(e_1\in T_1\), there exists an arc \(e_2\in T_2\) such that \((T_1\setminus\{e_1\})\cup\{e_2\}\) is a spanning tree of \(G\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Given two spanning trees of a connected graph, any arc removed from the first can be replaced by an arc from the second so that the resulting set is again a spanning tree.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists e_2\in T_2:\quad (T_1\setminus\{e_1\})\cup\{e_2\}\in\mathcal T(G).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Spanning Tree, Tree Edges, and Nontree Edges
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition, size property, and edge terminology for spanning trees.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A tree $T$ is a spanning tree of a graph $G$ if $T$ is a spanning subgraph of $G$. If $G$ is connected and has $n$ vertices, then every spanning tree of $G$ has $n-1$ edges. The edges in $T$ are called tree edges, and the edges of $G$ not in $T$ are called nontree edges.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A spanning tree of G is a tree that contains every vertex of G. In a connected n-vertex graph it has n minus one edges. Its edges are tree edges, and the remaining graph edges are nontree edges.
assumptions_latex: $T$ is a tree and a subgraph of $G$.
For the size assertion, $G$ is connected and has $n$ vertices.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T\text{ is a spanning tree of }G\iff V(T)=V(G);\qquad |E(T)|=n-1.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Cycles, trees, subnetworks, and spanning trees
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Foundational definitions for spanning structures, using the source's previously defined orientation-ignoring notion of path.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A cycle is a path \((n_1,\ldots,n_k)\) for which \(n_k=n_1\). A network is acyclic if it contains no cycle, and it is a tree if it is connected and acyclic. A network \((\widetilde{\mathcal N},\widetilde{\mathcal A})\) is a subnetwork of \((\mathcal N,\mathcal A)\) when \(\widetilde{\mathcal N}\subseteq\mathcal N\) and \(\widetilde{\mathcal A}\subseteq\mathcal A\). The subnetwork is a spanning tree when it is a tree and \(\widetilde{\mathcal N}=\mathcal N\). Relative to the fixed underlying network, a spanning tree can therefore be identified by its arc set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cycle is a path returning to its first node. An acyclic network contains no cycle, and a tree is connected and acyclic. A subnetwork uses subsets of the original nodes and arcs. It is a spanning tree when it is a tree containing every original node, so within a fixed network its arc set identifies it.
assumptions_latex: (\widetilde{\mathcal N},\widetilde{\mathcal A})\text{ is a candidate subnetwork of }(\mathcal N,\mathcal A).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (\widetilde{\mathcal N},\widetilde{\mathcal A})\text{ is a spanning tree}\iff \widetilde{\mathcal N}=\mathcal N\text{ and }(\widetilde{\mathcal N},\widetilde{\mathcal A})\text{ is connected and acyclic.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Incidence-Matrix Bases Characterize Spanning Trees
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded algebraic characterization of spanning trees in a connected digraph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a connected digraph, and let \(A=\{a_e:e\in E\}\) be its incidence matrix. For \(T\subseteq E\), the set \(\{a_e:e\in T\}\) is a column basis of \(A\) if and only if \(T\) is the arc set of a spanning tree of \(G\).

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \{a_e:e\in T\}\text{ is a column basis of }A\iff T\text{ is the arc set of a spanning tree of }G

knowledge_statements.title: Spanning Forests
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Includes nonmaximal spanning forests; maximality is characterized separately.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite undirected graph. A set \(F\subseteq E\) is a spanning forest of \(G\) if the spanning subgraph \((V,F)\) is acyclic; isolated vertices are retained. It is a maximal spanning forest if no edge of \(E\setminus F\) can be added without creating a cycle. Equivalently, a spanning forest is maximal if and only if it restricts to a spanning tree on every connected component of \(G\), or, equivalently, if and only if \(|F|=|V|-c(G)\), where \(c(G)\) is the number of connected components of \(G\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A spanning forest is an acyclic edge set on all vertices. Such a forest is maximal precisely when it spans each connected component by a tree, equivalently when it has |V|-c(G) edges.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \((V,F)\) is acyclic, then \(F\) is maximal acyclic exactly when \(|F|=|V|-c(G)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Directed In-Tree
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A tree whose edges are oriented toward a designated root.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A tree $T$ rooted at $s$ is a directed in-tree if, for every vertex $v\neq s$, the unique path in $T$ from $v$ to $s$ is directed from $v$ to $s$. Consequently, every vertex other than $s$ has outdegree $1$ in $T$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A tree rooted at s is a directed in-tree when the unique path from every other vertex to s is directed toward s. Every nonroot vertex then has outdegree one.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T\text{ is a directed in-tree}\iff \forall v\neq s,\text{ the unique }v\text{-}s\text{ path is directed from }v\text{ to }s;\qquad \deg_T^+(v)=1\quad\forall v\neq s.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Acyclic digraphs, rooted directed trees, arborescences, and branchings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines directed trees and forests and their spanning arc-set forms; also records the source–sink property of nonempty finite acyclic digraphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A digraph is acyclic if it has no directed circuit. Every nonempty finite acyclic digraph has at least one source and at least one sink. A directed tree is a digraph whose underlying undirected graph is a tree. It is rooted if it has precisely one source $r$; then every vertex $v\ne r$ has indegree $1$, and every vertex $v$ is joined to $r$ by a unique directed $r$-$v$ path. For $D=(V,A)$, an arborescence is a set $B\subseteq A$ such that $(V,B)$ is a rooted tree. A directed forest has an underlying undirected forest and is rooted if each weak component is a rooted tree. A branching is a set $B\subseteq A$ such that $(V,B)$ is a rooted forest.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An acyclic digraph has no directed circuit; if it is nonempty and finite, it has a source and a sink. A rooted directed tree has one source, and every other vertex has indegree one and a unique directed path from the root. An arborescence is a spanning rooted directed tree, while a branching is a spanning rooted directed forest.
assumptions_latex: B\subseteq A\text{ for the arborescence and branching definitions}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: D\text{ acyclic and }V\ne\varnothing\Rightarrow D\text{ has a source and a sink};\qquad B\text{ is an arborescence}\iff (V,B)\text{ is a rooted tree};\qquad B\text{ is a branching}\iff (V,B)\text{ is a rooted forest}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Directed Out-Tree
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A tree whose edges are oriented away from a designated root.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A tree $T$ rooted at $s$ is a directed out-tree if, for every vertex $v\neq s$, the unique path in $T$ from $s$ to $v$ is directed from $s$ to $v$. Consequently, every vertex other than $s$ has indegree $1$ in $T$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A tree rooted at s is a directed out-tree when the unique path from s to every other vertex is directed away from s. Every nonroot vertex then has indegree one.

knowledge_statements.title: In-Arborescences
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rooted spanning orientation directed toward the root.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D=(V,A)\) be a finite digraph and let \(r\in V\). An in-arborescence rooted at \(r\) is an arc set \(B\subseteq A\) whose underlying undirected graph is a spanning tree and in which every vertex \(v\in V\setminus\{r\}\) has outdegree one, while \(r\) has outdegree zero. Equivalently, \(|B|=|V|-1\) and, for every \(v\in V\), there is a unique directed path in \((V,B)\) from \(v\) to \(r\).

assumptions_latex: \(D=(V,A)\) is a finite digraph and \(r\in V\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(B\) is an in-arborescence rooted at \(r\) exactly when its arcs form a spanning tree directed toward \(r\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Rooted arborescences and rooted cuts
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Foundational definitions for an outward arborescence rooted at a fixed vertex and the associated cuts entering vertex sets not containing the root.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $D=(V,A)$ be a digraph and let $r\in V$. A set $A'\subseteq A$ is an $r$-arborescence if its arcs form a spanning tree and every vertex in $V\setminus\{r\}$ is the head of exactly one arc in $A'$. Hence, for every $s\in V$, $A'$ contains a unique directed path from $r$ to $s$. A set $C\subseteq A$ is an $r$-cut if $C=\delta^-(V')$ for some nonempty set $V'\subseteq V\setminus\{r\}$. One $r$-cut may contain another, and inclusionwise minimal $r$-cuts may therefore be considered.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a digraph with fixed root r, an r-arborescence is a spanning tree in which every nonroot vertex is the head of exactly one selected arc. It has a unique directed path from r to every vertex. An r-cut is the set of arcs entering a nonempty vertex set that does not contain r. Rooted cuts may contain one another, so inclusionwise minimal rooted cuts are sometimes distinguished.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A'\text{ is an }r\text{-arborescence}\iff A'\text{ forms a spanning tree and every }v\in V\setminus\{r\}\text{ is the head of exactly one arc in }A';\qquad C\text{ is an }r\text{-cut}\iff \exists\,\varnothing\ne V'\subseteq V\setminus\{r\}\text{ such that }C=\delta^-(V').

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Branchings and rooted out-arborescences
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definitions using the convention that arcs of a rooted arborescence point away from its root.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A digraph \(G\) is a branching if its underlying undirected graph is a forest and \(|\delta^-(v)|\leq 1\) for every \(v\in V(G)\). A connected branching is an arborescence. If such an arborescence has \(n\geq1\) vertices, then it has \(n-1\) edges and exactly one vertex \(r\) satisfying \(\delta^-(r)=\varnothing\); this vertex is its root. If \((v,w)\) is an edge, then \(w\) is a child of \(v\), while \(v\) is the parent or predecessor of \(w\). A vertex without children is a leaf.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A branching has a forest as its underlying undirected graph and at most one entering arc at each vertex. A connected branching is an outward arborescence. Every nonempty such arborescence has n−1 arcs and a unique indegree-zero root. Arc heads are children of their tails, tails are their parents or predecessors, and vertices without children are leaves.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: G\text{ is a branching}\iff \underline{G}\text{ is a forest and }|\delta^-(v)|\leq1\ \forall v;\quad G\text{ connected branching}\Rightarrow |E(G)|=n-1\text{ and }G\text{ has a unique root.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Equivalent characterizations of a rooted out-arborescence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural, rooted-reachability, minimality, cut, unique-walk, and indegree characterizations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\) be a digraph with \(|V(G)|=n\), and let \(r\in V(G)\). The following are equivalent: (a) \(G\) is an arborescence rooted at \(r\), meaning a connected branching with \(\delta^-(r)=\varnothing\); (b) \(G\) is a branching with \(n-1\) edges and \(\delta^-(r)=\varnothing\); (c) \(|E(G)|=n-1\) and every vertex is reachable from \(r\); (d) every vertex is reachable from \(r\), but deleting any edge destroys this property; (e) \(\delta^+(X)\neq\varnothing\) for every \(X\subsetneq V(G)\) with \(r\in X\), but deleting any edge destroys this property; (f) \(\delta^-(r)=\varnothing\) and there is a unique walk from \(r\) to every \(v\in V(G)\setminus\{r\}\); (g) \(\delta^-(r)=\varnothing\), \(|\delta^-(v)|=1\) for every \(v\neq r\), and \(G\) contains no circuit.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a digraph with root r, being an out-arborescence rooted at r is equivalent to being an n−1-edge branching with root indegree zero, having n−1 edges and reachability from r, being minimally root-reachable, satisfying the corresponding minimal outgoing-cut condition, having a unique walk from r to every other vertex, or satisfying the stated indegree and circuit conditions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (a)\iff(b)\iff(c)\iff(d)\iff(e)\iff(f)\iff(g).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Rooted Cuts and Rooted Out-Arborescences
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines rooted cuts and rooted spanning out-arborescences, states their inclusion-minimal cut-hitting characterization, and records the reachability condition for existence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $(D,\omega)$ be a weighted digraph and let $r\in V(D)$. For each nonempty $S\subseteq V(D)\setminus\{r\}$, the set $\delta^-(S)$ of arcs entering $S$ is an $r$-cut. An $r$-branching is a spanning arborescence oriented away from $r$. The inclusion-minimal arc sets meeting every $r$-cut are precisely the $r$-branchings. Moreover, an $r$-branching exists if and only if every vertex is reachable from $r$ by a directed path.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a weighted digraph rooted at r, an r-cut is the set of arcs entering a nonempty vertex set not containing r. An r-branching is a spanning arborescence directed away from r. The inclusion-minimal arc sets meeting every r-cut are exactly the r-branchings, and such a branching exists exactly when every vertex is reachable from r.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \{X\subseteq A(D):X\text{ is inclusion-minimal and }X\cap\delta^-(S)\neq\varnothing\ \forall\,\varnothing\neq S\subseteq V(D)\setminus\{r\}\}=\{B:B\text{ is a spanning out-arborescence rooted at }r\},\quad (\exists B)\iff(\forall v\in V(D),\ r\leadsto v).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Out-arborescence characterization and existence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the convention that arcs are directed away from the root; the branching definition is included as a prerequisite.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $D=(V,A)$ be a digraph. A branching is a set $B\subseteq A$ containing no undirected circuit and satisfying $|B\cap\delta^{\mathrm{in}}(v)|\leq 1$ for every $v\in V$. A branching is an arborescence when $(V,B)$ is weakly connected. Such a branching has a unique root $r$, and it is an $r$-arborescence equivalently when it is a directed spanning tree in which every vertex is reachable from $r$. Moreover, $D$ contains an $r$-arborescence if and only if every vertex of $D$ is reachable from $r$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A branching is an undirected-acyclic arc set with at most one selected arc entering each vertex. A weakly connected branching is an outward arborescence with a unique root. It is rooted at r exactly when every vertex is reachable from r in the selected directed spanning tree, and such a tree exists in the digraph exactly when every vertex is reachable from r.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: D\text{ contains an }r\text{-arborescence}\iff \forall v\in V,\;v\text{ is reachable from }r\text{ in }D.

knowledge_statements.title: Orientation Duality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Arc reversal exchanges the two rooted arborescence orientations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite digraph \(D=(V,A)\), define its reversal by \(D^{\mathrm{rev}}=(V,A^{\mathrm{rev}})\), where \(A^{\mathrm{rev}}=\{(v,u):(u,v)\in A\}\). For \(B\subseteq A\), let \(B^{\mathrm{rev}}\) contain the reversals of all arcs in \(B\). Then, for every root \(r\in V\), \(B\) is an out-arborescence of \(D\) rooted at \(r\) if and only if \(B^{\mathrm{rev}}\) is an in-arborescence of \(D^{\mathrm{rev}}\) rooted at \(r\). Reversal is an involution and hence a bijection between these families.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Reversing every arc bijectively converts rooted out-arborescences into rooted in-arborescences and preserves the root.
assumptions_latex: \(D=(V,A)\) is a finite digraph and \(r\in V\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(B\text{ is an out-arborescence at }r\iff B^{\mathrm{rev}}\text{ is an in-arborescence at }r\).

notation.meaning: digraph obtained by reversing every arc of D
arcwise reversal of B

knowledge_statements.title: Branchings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the indegree-bounded, outward-oriented convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D=(V,A)\) be a finite digraph. A branching is an arc set \(B\subseteq A\) such that the underlying undirected graph of \((V,B)\) is a forest and every vertex has indegree at most one in \((V,B)\). Each nontrivial component is therefore an out-arborescence rooted at its unique vertex of indegree zero; isolated vertices are roots of trivial components. knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A branching is an undirected forest whose arcs point outward from one root in each component, so every vertex has indegree at most one.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(B\subseteq A\) is a branching exactly when its underlying graph is a forest and \(d_B^-(v)\leq 1\) for every \(v\in V\).

knowledge_statements.title: Cobranchings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Arc-reversed counterpart of the chosen branching convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D=(V,A)\) be a finite digraph. A cobranching is an arc set \(C\subseteq A\) such that the underlying undirected graph of \((V,C)\) is a forest and every vertex has outdegree at most one in \((V,C)\). Each nontrivial component is therefore an in-arborescence rooted at its unique vertex of outdegree zero; isolated vertices are roots of trivial components. Thus a cobranching is a vertex-disjoint spanning collection of inward-oriented rooted trees.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C\subseteq A\) is a cobranching exactly when its underlying graph is a forest and \(d_C^+(v)\leq 1\) for every \(v\in V\).

knowledge_statements.title: Arc-Reversal Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Arc reversal exchanges branching and cobranching families.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D=(V,A)\) be a finite digraph and let \(D^{\mathrm{rev}}\) be obtained by reversing every arc. The map \(B\mapsto B^{\mathrm{rev}}\) preserves the underlying undirected forest and changes each indegree in \(B\) into the corresponding outdegree in \(B^{\mathrm{rev}}\). Consequently, \(B\) is a branching of \(D\) if and only if \(B^{\mathrm{rev}}\) is a cobranching of \(D^{\mathrm{rev}}\). Since arc reversal is involutive, this correspondence is a bijection and preserves cardinality and component vertex sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Reversing all selected arcs bijectively maps branchings to cobranchings while preserving their undirected forest, size, and components.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(B\text{ is a branching of }D\iff B^{\mathrm{rev}}\text{ is a cobranching of }D^{\mathrm{rev}}\).

notation.meaning: arc-reversed digraph
arcwise reversal of B

knowledge_statements.title: Graphic-Matroid Bases
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bases of the cycle matroid for possibly disconnected graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\), the graphic matroid \(M(G)\) has ground set \(E\) and independent sets equal to the edge sets containing no cycle. Its bases are precisely the inclusion-maximal forests of \(G\). Every basis \(B\) restricts to a spanning tree of each connected component of \(G\), and every such componentwise spanning forest is a basis. Hence all bases have cardinality \(r(M(G))=|V|-c(G)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Graphic-matroid bases are exactly maximal forests: they contain a spanning tree of every connected component and have size vertices minus components.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(B\text{ is a basis of }M(G)\iff B\text{ is a maximal forest of }G\).

notation.meaning: graphic or cycle matroid of G
number of connected components of G

knowledge_statements.title: Forest Independence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Graphic-matroid independence represented by acyclic edge sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite undirected graph and let \(M(G)\) be its graphic matroid. For every \(I\subseteq E\), the set \(I\) is independent in \(M(G)\) if and only if the spanning subgraph \((V,I)\) is a forest. Consequently, the circuits of \(M(G)\) are exactly the edge sets of cycles of \(G\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An edge set is independent in the graphic matroid exactly when it is a forest; the matroid circuits are precisely the edge sets of graph cycles.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(I\in\mathcal I(M(G))\iff (V,I)\text{ is a forest}\).

knowledge_statements.title: Basis–Tree Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Connected-graph specialization of graphic-matroid bases.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite connected undirected graph and let \(M(G)\) be its graphic matroid. An edge set \(T\subseteq E\) is a basis of \(M(G)\) if and only if \((V,T)\) is a spanning tree of \(G\). Thus the identity map on edge subsets gives a bijection between the bases of \(M(G)\) and the spanning trees of \(G\). In particular, every basis and every spanning tree has cardinality \(|V|-1\).

knowledge_statements.title: Arborescences as Common Matroid Bases
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fixed-root out-arborescences as common bases on the arc set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D=(V,A)\) be a finite digraph with root \(r\), and suppose loops are excluded. Let \(M_g\) be the graphic matroid on \(A\) obtained by forgetting arc orientations, retaining parallel edges. Let \(M_r\) be the partition matroid whose independent sets contain no arc entering \(r\) and at most one arc entering each \(v\in V\setminus\{r\}\). After deleting arcs entering \(r\), both matroids have rank \(|V|-1\) whenever an out-arborescence rooted at \(r\) exists. Then \(B\subseteq A\) is such an out-arborescence if and only if \(B\) is a common basis of \(M_g\) and \(M_r\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fixed-root out-arborescence is exactly a common basis of an underlying graphic matroid and a partition matroid enforcing one entering arc per nonroot vertex.
assumptions_latex: \(D=(V,A)\) is a finite loopless digraph with root \(r\in V\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(B\text{ is an out-arborescence rooted at }r\iff B\text{ is a common basis of }M_g\text{ and }M_r\).

notation.meaning: graphic matroid obtained by forgetting arc orientations

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strongly polynomial convex decomposition of a forest-polytope point
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Constructive representation by incidence vectors of forests.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\chi^T\in\{0,1\}^E\) denote the incidence vector of a spanning tree \(T\), let \(P_{\mathrm{ST}}(G)=\operatorname{conv}\{\chi^T:T\in\mathcal T(G)\}\), and let \(\tau=\min\{w^\top x:x\in P_{\mathrm{ST}}(G)\}\). The optimal set \[F_w=\{x\in P_{\mathrm{ST}}(G):w^\top x=\tau\}\] is an exposed face of the spanning-tree polytope, and \[F_w=\operatorname{conv}\{\chi^T:T\in\mathcal T(G),\ w^\top\chi^T=\tau\}.\] Its vertices are precisely the incidence vectors of minimum spanning trees. Consequently, the optimum is unique exactly when \(F_w\) is a singleton vertex; otherwise the optimal face has positive dimension.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each \(f\in T\), deleting \(f\) splits \(T\) into two vertex sets; let \(\delta_T(f)\) be the set of graph edges crossing that cut. Then \(T\) is a minimum spanning tree if and only if \[w(f)=\min\{w(e):e\in\delta_T(f)\}\qquad(f\in T).\] The collection of these \(|V|-1\) comparisons is an optimality certificate: the tree supplies the fundamental cuts, and direct weight comparisons verify that every selected edge is a cut minimum. Then \(T^*\) is a minimum spanning tree if and only if, for every edge \(e\in T^*\), \(c_e\le c_f\) for every edge \(f\) crossing the cut formed by deleting \(e\) from \(T^*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A spanning tree is minimum if and only if each tree edge is a cheapest edge across the cut created by deleting it.

T^*\subseteq E\text{ is a spanning tree of }G.

The cut \((S,V\setminus S)\) respects \(A\), and \(e\in\delta(S)\) has minimum weight among all edges of \(\delta(S)\).

If \(e\in\delta(S)\) satisfies \(w(e)=\min\{w(f):f\in\delta(S)\}\), then \(e\) is safe for \(A\): some minimum spanning tree contains every edge of \(A\cup\{e\}\).

children.title: Tied Cut Minima
children.top_down_role: Certificate behavior when several edges attain the same minimum cut weight.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite, connected, undirected weighted graph.
\(A\subseteq E\) is contained in some minimum spanning tree, and \(A\cap\delta(S)=\varnothing\).
Distinct edges \(e_1,e_2\in\delta(S)\) attain the same minimum cut weight.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each \(e_i\) is individually safe for \(A\), but the pair \(\{e_1,e_2\}\) need not be jointly safe.

notation.meaning: The set of edges crossing the cut defined by S.
A forest extendible to a minimum spanning tree.

The trees \(T_1\) and \(T_2\) may differ. In particular, tied cut minima do not imply that one minimum spanning tree contains all tied edges; their simultaneous inclusion may create a cycle or otherwise prevent extension.

knowledge_statements.title: Cut-Certificate Failure Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A concrete boundary showing that merely crossing a cut does not certify safe inclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the cut \((\{a\},\{b,c\})\), both \(ab\) and \(ac\) cross, but \(w(ab)>w(ac)\). The unique minimum spanning tree is \(\{ac,bc\}\), of weight \(2\); every spanning tree containing \(ab\) has weight at least \(3\). Thus a crossing edge that is not a cut minimum cannot be declared safe by the cut certificate.

The spanning tree \(T\) is a minimum spanning tree exactly when \(w(e)\geq w(f)\) for every \(e\in E\setminus T\) and every \(f\in P_T(e)\). These inequalities are directly checkable and constitute a cycle-based optimality certificate for \(T\).

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite, connected, undirected weighted graph.
An edge \(e\in C\) satisfies \(w(e)>w(f)\) for every \(f\in C\setminus\{e\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: No minimum spanning tree of \(G\) contains \(e\).

notation.meaning: A cycle of the graph.
The unique strictly heaviest edge of C.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: The strict cycle property, which excludes an edge from every minimum spanning tree.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\) be any cycle of \(G\). If \(e\in C\) is its unique maximum-weight edge, meaning \(w(e)>w(f)\) for all \(f\in C\setminus\{e\}\), then \(e\) is excluded from every minimum spanning tree. Hence the cycle together with the strict weight comparisons is a verifiable certificate that \(e\) cannot occur in an optimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An edge that is uniquely heaviest on a cycle is absent from every minimum spanning tree.

children.title: Tied Cycle Maxima
children.top_down_role: Certificate behavior when several cycle edges share the maximum weight.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite, connected, undirected weighted graph.
\(C\) is a cycle and \(e\in C\) attains \(\max\{w(f):f\in C\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Some minimum spanning tree excludes \(e\), but tied maximality alone does not exclude \(e\) from every minimum spanning tree.

notation.meaning: A cycle containing the maximal edge.
An edge attaining the maximum weight on C.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes existential exclusion under ties from universal exclusion under a strict maximum.

source_refs.locator: Section 6.1. Minimum Spanning Trees p. 134

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(w(e)=\max\{w(f):f\in C\}\), then there exists at least one minimum spanning tree that does not contain \(e\). If another edge of \(C\) has the same maximum weight, the stronger universal-exclusion conclusion can fail. For example, when all three edges of a triangle have equal weight, every edge is a tied cycle maximum, yet each edge belongs to some minimum spanning tree and is omitted by another.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A tied maximum on a cycle can be omitted from an optimum, but it may also occur in another optimum.

knowledge_statements.title: Cycle-Certificate Failure Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A concrete boundary showing that cycle membership without maximality gives no exclusion certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In the cycle \(C=\{ab,ac,bc\}\), the edge \(ab\) is not maximum because \(w(ab)=1<2=w(ac)=w(bc)\). Every minimum spanning tree has weight \(3\) and contains \(ab\) together with exactly one of \(ac\) and \(bc\). Thus an edge cannot be certified as excludable merely because it lies on a cycle; maximality is essential, and strict maximality is required for exclusion from every optimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonmaximal cycle edge may occur in every optimum; strict maximality is needed for universal exclusion.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The nonmaximal cycle edge \(ab\) belongs to every minimum spanning tree, so its cycle cannot certify exclusion.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Adding \(e\) to \(T\) creates the unique cycle \(P_T(e)\cup\{e\}\). For every \(f\in P_T(e)\), deleting \(f\) yields the spanning tree \(T-f+e\). Conversely, if \(T-g+e\) is a spanning tree for some \(g\in T\), then \(g\in P_T(e)\). Thus the fundamental path identifies precisely all single-edge exchanges that insert \(e\) while preserving the spanning-tree property.

children.title: Basis Exchange Structure
children.top_down_role: Matroidal exchange relations among graphic-matroid bases.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite, connected, undirected graph.
\(M(G)\) is its graphic matroid, whose independent sets are forests.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The bases of \(M(G)\) are exactly the spanning trees, and they satisfy symmetric basis exchange.

notation.meaning: The graphic matroid of G.
Two bases, equivalently two spanning trees.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Identifies spanning trees with graphic-matroid bases and states their exchange law.

source_refs.locator: Section 6.1. Minimum Spanning Trees p. 134

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A set \(B\subseteq E\) is a basis of \(M(G)\) if and only if \(B\) is a spanning tree of \(G\). Moreover, for any bases \(B_1,B_2\) and any \(e\in B_1\setminus B_2\), there exists \(f\in B_2\setminus B_1\) such that both \(B_1-e+f\) and \(B_2-f+e\) are bases. Hence graph-theoretic tree exchanges realize symmetric matroid basis exchange.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Spanning trees are precisely graphic-matroid bases, and exchanges between two trees realize the symmetric basis-exchange property.

children.title: Fundamental-Cycle Exchanges
children.top_down_role: Tree substitutions organized through cycles created by entering edges.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite, connected, undirected graph with weights \(w:E\to\mathbb{R}\).
\(T\) is a minimum spanning tree, \(e\in E\setminus T\), and \(f\in P_T(e)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The exchange \(T-f+e\) is a spanning tree with weight \(w(T)+w(e)-w(f)\), and it is minimum if and only if \(w(e)=w(f)\).

notation.meaning: The unique tree path joining the endpoints of e.
The sum of weights of edges in T.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weighted exchanges along a fundamental cycle of an already optimal tree.

source_refs.locator: Section 6.1. Minimum Spanning Trees p. 134

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The set \(T'=T-f+e\) is a spanning tree and satisfies \(w(T')=w(T)+w(e)-w(f)\). Since \(T\) is minimum, \(w(f)\leq w(e)\) for every \(f\in P_T(e)\). Consequently, \(T'\) is also a minimum spanning tree exactly when \(w(f)=w(e)\); a strict inequality \(w(f)<w(e)\) makes the exchanged tree strictly heavier.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fundamental-cycle exchange preserves optimality exactly when the inserted and removed edges have equal weight.

children.top_down_role: Recognition and certification of a proposed optimum.

\(T\subseteq E\) is a proposed spanning tree.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The inequalities \(w(e)\geq\max\{w(f):f\in P_T(e)\}\) for all \(e\in E\setminus T\) certify that \(T\) is a minimum spanning tree.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Verify first that \(T\) is connected and has \(|V|-1\) edges. For every \(e\in E\setminus T\), compute the maximum edge weight on \(P_T(e)\). knowledge_statements.statement_title: Equivalent optimality certificates for a minimum spanning tree
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent path, fundamental-cut, and admissible edge-order characterizations of minimum-spanning-tree optimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((G,c)\) be an instance of the minimum spanning tree problem, let \(T\) be a spanning tree of \(G\), and let \(n=|V(G)|\). The following are equivalent: (a) \(T\) is optimal; (b) for every \(e=\{x,y\}\in E(G)\setminus E(T)\), every edge \(a\) on the \(x\)-\(y\) path in \(T\) satisfies \(c(a)\leq c(e)\); (c) for every \(e\in E(T)\), if \(C\) is a connected component of \(T-e\), then \(e\) is a minimum-cost edge of \(\delta(V(C))\); (d) the edges can be ordered as \(E(T)=\{e_1,\ldots,e_{n-1}\}\) so that for every \(i\) there is an \(X\subseteq V(G)\) for which \(e_i\) is a minimum-cost edge of \(\delta(X)\) and \(e_j\notin\delta(X)\) for all \(j<i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A spanning tree is minimum-weight exactly when it satisfies the path condition for every non-tree edge, equivalently the fundamental-cut condition for every tree edge, equivalently the stated cut-compatible ordering condition.
assumptions_latex: (G,c)\text{ is an instance of the minimum spanning tree problem}
T\text{ is a spanning tree of }G
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathrm{(a)}\iff\mathrm{(b)}\iff\mathrm{(c)}\iff\mathrm{(d)}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Descending-Weight Kruskal Algorithm for a Maximum Spanning Tree
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Maximum-weight objective specialization of the classical cycle-avoiding spanning-tree greedy algorithm.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $G_r$ be the complete undirected graph on vertices $\{1,\ldots,m\}$, with edge $\{i,j\}$ weighted by $r_{ij}$. Process the edges in nonincreasing order of weight, breaking ties arbitrarily. Accept an edge if its addition to the accepted set creates no cycle, and stop after accepting $m-1$ edges. The accepted edges form a maximum-total-weight spanning tree of $G_r$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Process the edges from largest to smallest weight, accepting an edge whenever it does not create a cycle. After m−1 edges have been accepted, they form a maximum-weight spanning tree.

\text{edges are processed in nonincreasing weight order}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T_r\in\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{T\text{ spanning tree of }G_r}\sum_{\{i,j\}\in T}r_{ij}

knowledge_statements.title: Dense-Graph Implementations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Array-based Jarník–Prim implementation for a connected dense undirected graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a connected undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\) with \(n=|V|\), edge weights \(w:E\to\mathbb R\), and root \(r\), initialize \(S=\{r\}\), \(d(r)=0\), and \(d(v)=w(rv)\) when \(rv\in E\), otherwise \(d(v)=+\infty\). Repeatedly scan every vertex in \(V\setminus S\), choose one minimizing \(d(v)\), add its recorded predecessor edge to \(T\), insert \(v\) into \(S\), and update \(d(u)=\min\{d(u),w(uv)\}\) for all \(u\notin S\). When \(S=V\), output \(T\). The output is a minimum spanning tree, using \(O(n^2)\) weight comparisons and \(O(n)\) auxiliary storage when adjacency-matrix access is constant-time.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Array-based Prim repeatedly scans all unchosen vertices for the cheapest crossing edge, producing a minimum spanning tree in quadratic time.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The returned edge set \(T\) is a minimum spanning tree and is computed in \(O(n^2)\) time.

notation.meaning: vertices already incorporated into the tree

knowledge_statements.title: Priority-Queue Implementations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Heap-based Jarník–Prim implementation emphasizing sparse-graph complexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a connected undirected weighted graph \(G=(V,E)\) and root \(r\), assign keys \(d(r)=0\) and \(d(v)=+\infty\) for \(v\ne r\), and place all vertices in a min-priority queue. Repeatedly extract a vertex \(v\) of minimum key, append its predecessor edge when \(v\ne r\), and for each unextracted neighbor \(u\) with \(w(uv)<d(u)\), set \(d(u)=w(uv)\), record predecessor \(v\), and perform decrease-key. The resulting edges form a minimum spanning tree. With adjacency lists and a binary heap the running time is \(O((|V|+|E|)\log |V|)\), customarily \(O(|E|\log |V|)\) for connected graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Heap-based Prim maintains the cheapest attachment key per unchosen vertex and constructs a minimum spanning tree efficiently on sparse graphs.
assumptions_latex: The queue supports extract-min and decrease-key.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The algorithm returns a minimum spanning tree in \(O((|V|+|E|)\log |V|)\) time with a binary heap.

notation.meaning: current attachment key of vertex v

knowledge_statements.title: Disjoint-Set Implementations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Kruskal implementation using union–find for component maintenance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a finite undirected weighted graph \(G=(V,E)\), make one disjoint-set singleton for each vertex, sort the edges into nondecreasing weight order, and initialize \(F=\varnothing\). For each edge \(uv\) in that order, test whether \(\operatorname{Find}(u)\ne\operatorname{Find}(v)\). If so, set \(F\leftarrow F\cup\{uv\}\) and apply \(\operatorname{Union}(u,v)\); otherwise discard the edge. The output is a minimum-weight spanning forest, and it is a minimum spanning tree when \(G\) is connected. Union by rank and path compression perform all disjoint-set operations in \(O((|V|+|E|)\alpha(|V|))\) time after sorting.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Kruskal uses union–find to accept an edge exactly when it joins different current components, yielding a minimum spanning forest.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\) is a minimum-weight spanning forest; if \(G\) is connected, \(F\) is a minimum spanning tree.

notation.meaning: accepted forest
inverse Ackermann function

knowledge_statements.title: Parallel Forest-Merging Variants
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weight-batched Kruskal variant permitting parallel processing without unsafe cyclic merges.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Partition \(E\) into batches \(E_1,\ldots,E_k\) of equal weight, ordered by increasing weight. Before batch \(E_i\), contract every component of the forest \(F\) selected from earlier batches. In parallel, discard edges of \(E_i\) whose endpoints contract to the same vertex; on the resulting quotient multigraph choose any spanning forest \(H_i\), and lift its edges into \(F\). Then contract the new components and continue. Edges within \(H_i\) may be selected by any correct parallel spanning-forest routine. After all batches, \(F\) is a minimum-weight spanning forest of \(G\), and is a minimum spanning tree when \(G\) is connected.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Equal-weight edges are processed on the quotient of lighter-edge components; a parallel spanning forest of each batch safely merges components.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite undirected weighted graph.
Each batch routine returns a spanning forest of its quotient graph.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The accumulated set \(F\) is a minimum-weight spanning forest of \(G\).

notation.meaning: one equal-weight edge batch
forest selected in the batch quotient graph
accumulated forest

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The weight-batched quotient-forest construction is plausible and fits the leaf, but it lacks an authoritative source. No parallel computation model or complexity claim is fixed, so its precise status as a parallel variant also requires sourcing.

knowledge_statements.title: Borůvka Component-Contraction Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical Borůvka phases with componentwise light-edge selection and contraction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize \(F=\varnothing\), with each vertex of a connected undirected weighted graph \(G=(V,E)\) forming one component. In each phase, every current component \(C\) chooses a minimum-weight edge crossing \(\delta(C)\). Add a cycle-free maximal subset of the chosen edges to \(F\), merge their incident components, and equivalently contract the resulting components. Continue until one component remains. Every accepted edge is safe for some minimum spanning tree, so the final \(F\) is a minimum spanning tree. With consistent handling of duplicate choices, each nonterminal phase reduces the number of components by at least a factor of two, giving at most \(\lceil\log_2 |V|\rceil\) phases.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Borůvka repeatedly chooses a cheapest outgoing edge for every component and contracts the resulting forest, obtaining an MST in logarithmically many phases.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The algorithm returns a minimum spanning tree after at most \(\lceil\log_2 |V|\rceil\) nonterminal phases.

notation.meaning: accumulated selected forest

children.title: Reverse-Delete Methods
children.top_down_role: Cycle-driven deletion approaches for retaining a minimum spanning tree.

knowledge_statements.title: Reverse-Delete Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Descending-weight deletion algorithm for a connected undirected graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a connected undirected weighted graph \(G=(V,E)\), initialize \(H=G\) and order the edges by nonincreasing weight. Process each edge \(e\) once in that order. If \(H-e\) remains connected, replace \(H\) by \(H-e\); otherwise retain \(e\). After every edge has been considered, output \(E(H)\). The final graph is connected and contains no cycle, since the heaviest remaining edge of any cycle would have been deletable when processed. Consequently \(H\) is a spanning tree, and the cycle property implies that it has minimum total weight.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Reverse-delete examines edges from heaviest to lightest and removes an edge whenever connectivity survives; the remaining graph is an MST.
assumptions_latex: Edges are processed in nonincreasing weight order.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The remaining graph \(H\) is a minimum spanning tree of \(G\).

notation.meaning: current connected spanning subgraph
graph obtained by deleting edge e

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The reverse-delete algorithm fits the terminal container, but no inspectable citation is supplied. The statement also includes proof-style justification beginning with the cycle argument, contrary to the no-proof requirement.

children.title: Dual Greedy Viewpoint
children.top_down_role: Greedy interpretations based on removing edges rather than constructing a forest.

knowledge_statements.title: Dual Greedy Viewpoint
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reverse-delete as greedy maximization in the cographic matroid.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be connected and let \(M^*(G)\) be its cographic matroid. A set \(D\subseteq E\) is independent in \(M^*(G)\) exactly when \(G-D\) is connected. Thus reverse-delete, which scans edges by nonincreasing weight and inserts \(e\) into \(D\) whenever \(G-(D\cup\{e\})\) remains connected, is the ordinary maximum-weight greedy algorithm on \(M^*(G)\). At termination \(D\) is a maximum-weight cographic basis, while \(T=E\setminus D\) is a spanning tree. Since \(w(T)=w(E)-w(D)\), maximizing deleted weight is equivalent to minimizing retained tree weight.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Reverse-delete is maximum-weight matroid greedy on deletable edges; complementing the maximum-weight cographic basis gives a minimum spanning tree.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D\) is a maximum-weight basis of \(M^*(G)\) if and only if \(E\setminus D\) is a minimum spanning tree of \(G\).

notation.meaning: cographic matroid of G
deleted edge set
retained spanning tree

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The cographic-matroid interpretation is mathematically appropriate for the dual greedy viewpoint, but the independence characterization and complementary-basis claim require an authoritative matroid source with a specific locator.

children.title: Deletion-Order Variants
children.top_down_role: Ordering regimes for cycle-preserving edge removal.

knowledge_statements.title: Deletion-Order Variants
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Order invariance subject to the nonincreasing-weight constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be connected, and let \(\preceq\) be any total edge order satisfying \(w(e)>w(f)\Rightarrow e\) is processed before \(f\). Starting from \(G\), process edges according to \(\preceq\) and delete an edge precisely when its deletion preserves connectivity. The retained edge set is a minimum spanning tree. Hence arbitrary permutation within each equal-weight class, as well as any implementation that realizes such a linear order, preserves optimality. If the processing order violates the nonincreasing-weight condition, the guarantee fails: on a weighted cycle, deleting a lighter edge before a heavier deletable edge can leave a nonminimum spanning tree.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Any reverse-delete order descending by weight is valid, including arbitrary tie orders; processing lighter edges too early can destroy optimality.
assumptions_latex: The order is nonincreasing in edge weight.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every permitted deletion order returns a minimum spanning tree; unrestricted orders need not do so.

notation.meaning: total processing order on edges

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The order-invariance and failure-boundary claims fit the leaf and are stated consistently, but neither the reverse-delete result nor the counterexample claim has cited support.

children.title: Tied-Weight Deletion Regimes
children.top_down_role: Reverse-delete behavior when candidate edges have equal weights.

knowledge_statements.title: Tied-Weight Deletion Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Correctness and possible nonuniqueness under tied edge weights.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Partition the edges of a connected weighted graph into equal-weight classes and process the classes from greatest to least weight. Within a class, process edges in any order, deleting an edge exactly when the current graph remains connected. Every resulting retained set is a minimum spanning tree, although different within-class orders may produce different trees. All outputs have the same total weight. Distinct edge weights force a unique minimum spanning tree and therefore an order-independent output; with ties, uniqueness may still occur but is not guaranteed. Simultaneously deleting every individually deletable edge in a tied class is invalid unless their joint deletion is also verified to preserve connectivity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Tie order does not affect optimal weight but may change the returned MST; simultaneous deletions require a joint connectivity check.
assumptions_latex: Weight classes are processed from greatest to least.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Sequential tie-breaking always yields an MST, whereas uncoordinated simultaneous deletion can disconnect the graph.

notation.meaning: edges having common weight lambda

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The tied-weight behavior and warning about simultaneous deletion fit the leaf, but the record supplies no authoritative citation or locator.

children.title: Forest Polytope
children.top_down_role: The convex-hull model for acyclic edge sets.

knowledge_statements.title: Forest Polytope
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Independent-set polytope of the graphic matroid for a finite simple graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a finite simple undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\), let \(E(S)=\{uv\in E:u,v\in S\}\). The forest polytope is
\[P_{\mathrm{for}}(G)=\operatorname{conv}\{\chi^F\in\{0,1\}^E:F\subseteq E\text{ is acyclic}\}.\]
It has the exact linear description
\[P_{\mathrm{for}}(G)=\left\{x\in\mathbb R^E_{\ge 0}:x(E(S))\le |S|-1\text{ for every nonempty }S\subseteq V\right\}.\]
The singleton inequalities imply \(x_e\le 1\) by taking the two endpoints of \(e\). Every vertex of this polytope is therefore the incidence vector of a forest.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The forest polytope is the convex hull of acyclic edge sets and is described exactly by nonnegativity and induced-subgraph rank inequalities.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite simple undirected graph.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed rank-inequality system equals the convex hull of incidence vectors of forests in \(G\).

notation.meaning: edges induced by vertex set S

knowledge_statements.title: Spanning-Tree Polytopes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Edmonds-style description of the spanning-tree polytope.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a connected finite simple undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\), the spanning-tree polytope is
\[P_{\mathrm{ST}}(G)=\operatorname{conv}\{\chi^T:T\subseteq E\text{ is a spanning tree of }G\}.\]
It is exactly the face of the forest polytope having full graphic rank:
\[P_{\mathrm{ST}}(G)=\left\{x\in\mathbb R^E_{\ge0}:x(E)=|V|-1,\;x(E(S))\le |S|-1\text{ for every }\varnothing\ne S\subsetneq V\right\}.\]
Equivalently, using \(x(E)=|V|-1\), the rank inequalities may be expressed through appropriate partition or cut constraints. Its vertices are precisely the incidence vectors of spanning trees.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The spanning-tree polytope is the full-rank face of the forest polytope, defined by nonnegativity, total rank, and induced-subgraph inequalities.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is finite, simple, undirected, and connected.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed system is integral and equals \(P_{\mathrm{ST}}(G)\).

notation.meaning: spanning-tree polytope of G
edges induced by S
incidence vector of tree T

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The displayed spanning-tree polytope description is appropriate, but its exactness and integrality require a polyhedral source with a precise locator. The claimed equivalent partition or cut formulation is not actually stated.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Spanning-Tree Polytope Description and Integrality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Complete linear description of the spanning-tree polytope of a connected undirected graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G\) be a connected undirected graph and \(n=|V(G)|\). Then
\[
P=\left\{x\in[0,1]^{E(G)}:\sum_{e\in E(G)}x_e=n-1,\quad \sum_{e\in E(G[X])}x_e\le |X|-1\ \text{for every }\varnothing\ne X\subsetneq V(G)\right\}
\]
is integral, and its vertices are exactly the incidence vectors of the spanning trees of \(G\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For every connected undirected graph, the unit-cube vectors having total edge value n−1 and satisfying every proper nonempty induced-subgraph rank inequality form an integral polytope whose vertices are precisely the spanning-tree incidence vectors.
assumptions_latex: G\text{ is a connected undirected graph}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: P\text{ is integral and }\operatorname{vert}(P)=\{\chi^T:T\text{ is a spanning tree of }G\}.

children.title: Connector Polytopes

knowledge_statements.title: Connector Polytopes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex-hull model for connected spanning edge sets, without minimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a connected finite undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\), call \(C\subseteq E\) a connector when the spanning subgraph \((V,C)\) is connected. The connector polytope is
\[P_{\mathrm{con}}(G)=\operatorname{conv}\{\chi^C\in\{0,1\}^E:(V,C)\text{ is connected}\}.\]
Every point \(x\in P_{\mathrm{con}}(G)\) satisfies \(0\le x_e\le1\) for \(e\in E\) and \(x(\delta(S))\ge1\) for every \(\varnothing\ne S\subsetneq V\). Its incidence vectors are upward closed: if \(C\) is a connector and \(C\subseteq C'\subseteq E\), then \(C'\) is also a connector. Inclusion-minimal connectors are exactly spanning trees.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The connector polytope is the convex hull of connected spanning subgraphs; its inclusion-minimal incidence vectors are spanning trees.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P_{\mathrm{con}}(G)\) models all spanning connectors, and its inclusion-minimal generating sets are spanning trees.

notation.meaning: connector polytope of G
cut with exactly one endpoint in S
incidence vector of connector C

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition and minimal-connector characterization fit the connector-polytope leaf, but no authoritative source with a specific locator is supplied.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a graph \(G=(V,E)\), the connector polytope is \[P_{\mathrm{connector}}(G)=\left\{x\in[0,1]^E:x(\delta(\mathcal P))\ge |\mathcal P|-1\quad\text{for every partition }\mathcal P\text{ of }V\right\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The connector polytope consists exactly of edge vectors in the unit cube whose value on the edges crossing every vertex partition is at least the number of blocks minus one.
assumptions_latex: \delta(\mathcal P)=\{e\in E:e\text{ joins distinct blocks of }\mathcal P\}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: P_{\mathrm{connector}}(G)=\{x\in[0,1]^E:x(\delta(\mathcal P))\ge |\mathcal P|-1\ \forall\text{ partitions }\mathcal P\text{ of }V\}

children.title: Tree Faces of Connector Polytopes

knowledge_statements.title: Tree Faces of Connector Polytopes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The spanning-tree polytope is the minimum-cardinality face of the connected spanning-subgraph polytope.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a connected undirected graph, and let \(P_{\mathrm{con}}(G)=\operatorname{conv}\{\chi^F:F\subseteq E,\ (V,F)\text{ is connected}\}\). Every connected spanning edge set has at least \(|V|-1\) edges. Consequently, the valid inequality \(x(E)\ge |V|-1\) exposes the face \[P_{\mathrm{con}}(G)\cap\{x:x(E)=|V|-1\}=\operatorname{conv}\{\chi^T:T\text{ is a spanning tree of }G\}.\] Thus the minimum-cardinality connector face is precisely the spanning-tree polytope.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Among connected spanning subgraphs, exactly those having the minimum possible number of edges are spanning trees; their convex hull is an exposed face of the connector polytope.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P_{\mathrm{con}}(G)\cap\{x:x(E)=|V|-1\}=P_{\mathrm{ST}}(G)\).

notation.meaning: Incidence vector of the edge set F.
Sum of x_e over edges e in A.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property is mathematically precise, matches the tree-face container, and uses consistent notation, but no inspectable source with a specific locator is supplied.

children.title: Nonminimal Connector Regimes
children.top_down_role: Connected spanning edge sets containing edges beyond a spanning tree.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonminimal Connector Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonminimal connected subgraphs matter when edge costs are not nonnegative.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be connected and let \(c\in\mathbb{R}^E\). If \(c_e\ge0\) for every \(e\in E\), each connected spanning edge set \(F\) contains a spanning tree \(T\subseteq F\) satisfying \(c(T)\le c(F)\); hence an optimal connector can be chosen as a tree. This reduction fails with negative costs: on a triangle with \(c_e=-1\) for all three edges, the full three-edge connector has cost \(-3\), whereas every spanning tree has cost \(-2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nonnegative costs permit pruning an optimal connector to a tree. Negative costs can make a connected spanning subgraph with extra edges strictly better than every tree.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite connected undirected graph.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Nonminimal connectors are dispensable for \(c\ge0\), but not for unrestricted \(c\in\mathbb{R}^E\).

notation.meaning: Total edge cost over F.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The nonnegative-cost pruning statement and negative-cost triangle counterexample correctly express the nonminimal-connector boundary, but the record has no cited source with a specific locator.

children.title: Cut-Inequality Separation

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A violated connectivity cut exists if and only if \(\min_{\varnothing\ne S\subsetneq V}x(\delta(S))<1\).

notation.meaning: Edges with exactly one endpoint in S.
Sum of capacities x_e over A.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global minimum cut separates connectivity inequalities for fractional connector vectors.

source_refs.locator: Section 6. Linear Programming Interpretation of Max-Flow Min-Cut Theorem p. 123
Section 4.6. Separation and Optimization p. 93

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a finite undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\) with \(|V|\ge 2\) and a vector \(x\in\mathbb{Q}_{\ge0}^E\), assign capacity \(x_e\) to edge \(e\). Compute a nontrivial global minimum cut \(\delta(S)\), where \(\varnothing\ne S\subsetneq V\). If \(x(\delta(S))<1\), output the violated connector inequality \(x(\delta(S))\ge1\). Otherwise certify that every inequality \(x(\delta(U))\ge1\), for \(\varnothing\ne U\subsetneq V\), is satisfied. The oracle therefore requires one polynomial-time global minimum-cut computation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a graph with at least two vertices, a minimum-capacity nontrivial cut either supplies a violated connectivity inequality or certifies that every connectivity cut has capacity at least one.

children.title: Integral Spanning-Tree Optimization
children.top_down_role: Linear optimization over integral spanning-tree representations.

knowledge_statements.title: Integral Spanning-Tree Optimization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Edmonds' finite undirected spanning-tree polytope formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a connected undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\), define \[P=\{x\in\mathbb{R}_{\ge0}^E:x(E)=|V|-1,\ x(E(S))\le |S|-1\text{ for every }\varnothing\ne S\subsetneq V\}.\] Then \(P\) is integral and equals the convex hull of incidence vectors of spanning trees of \(G\). Hence, for every \(c\in\mathbb{Q}^E\), minimizing \(c^{\mathsf T}x\) over \(P\) has an integral optimal solution, and any such solution is the incidence vector of a minimum-cost spanning tree.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The subtour description of the spanning-tree polytope is integral, so linear optimization over it returns a minimum-cost spanning tree.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite connected undirected graph.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P=\operatorname{conv}\{\chi^T:T\text{ is a spanning tree of }G\}\), and \(\min_{x\in P}c^{\mathsf T}x\) has a tree-incidence optimum.

notation.meaning: Edges having both endpoints in S.
Incidence vector of tree T.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The stated finite undirected spanning-tree polytope theorem is precise and fits the integral-optimization container, but the claimed integrality and exact description require an authoritative Edmonds-type source with a specific theorem, section, or page locator.

children.title: Separation–Optimization Interface
children.top_down_role: Relationship between inequality separation and optimization access.

knowledge_statements.title: Separation–Optimization Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strong separation and strong linear optimization are polynomial-time oracle equivalent.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\) be a nonempty bounded rational polyhedron whose facet complexity and containing-radius data are polynomially bounded in the binary input description. A strong separation oracle for \(P\) yields, via the ellipsoid method, a polynomial-time algorithm that either optimizes \(c^{\mathsf T}x\) over \(P\) for rational \(c\) or reports \(P=\varnothing\). Conversely, a strong optimization oracle for \(P\) yields a polynomial-time strong separation oracle. Running time is polynomial in \(d\), the encoding lengths, and the relevant oracle complexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For suitably encoded rational polyhedra, exact separation and exact linear optimization can each be implemented in polynomial time using an oracle for the other.
assumptions_latex: \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\) is a rational polyhedron with polynomially controlled encoding data.
Oracle inputs and outputs use binary rational encoding.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Strong separation over \(P\) and strong linear optimization over \(P\) are polynomial-time oracle equivalent.

notation.meaning: Rational polyhedron under consideration.
Rational linear objective vector.

More importantly, the precise hypotheses needed for strong optimization-separation equivalence are expressed only vaguely as polynomially bounded encoding and radius data. children.title: Fractional Relaxation Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Behavior of spanning formulations when integral structure is not enforced.

knowledge_statements.title: Fractional Relaxation Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Connectivity cut inequalities alone do not describe the connector polytope.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=K_3\) and set \(x_e=\tfrac12\) for each of its three edges. Then \(0\le x_e\le1\) and every nontrivial cut has two crossing edges, so \(x(\delta(S))=1\). Thus \(x\) satisfies all connectivity cut inequalities. Nevertheless, every connected spanning subgraph of \(K_3\) has at least two edges, whereas \(x(E)=\tfrac32\). Hence \(x\) is not in the convex hull of connected spanning-subgraph incidence vectors, demonstrating that the cut relaxation is fractional.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Half an edge on every side of a triangle satisfies all connectivity cuts but lies outside the connector polytope because its total edge mass is below two.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\in\{y\in[0,1]^E:y(\delta(S))\ge1\}\) but \(x\notin P_{\mathrm{con}}(K_3)\).

notation.meaning: Convex hull of connected spanning-subgraph incidence vectors.
Cut induced by S.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The triangle vector is a valid explicit counterexample and the counterexample content kind fits the relaxation-boundary container, but no inspectable source locator is supplied for the claimed polyhedral boundary.

children.title: Comparison Decision-Tree Model Pair
