knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The bounded partial-coverage feasible family is
\[
\mathcal{B}_{[\ell,u]}(D)=\{F\subseteq A:F\text{ is a branching and }\ell\le |V(F)|\le u\}.
\]
A minimum- or maximum-weight partial-coverage problem optimizes \(w(F)=\sum_{a\in F}w(a)\) over this family. Exact coverage \(q\) is obtained by setting \(\ell=u=q\); unrestricted nonspanning coverage is obtained by taking \(\ell=0\) and \(u=|V|-1\). Feasibility depends on whether some branching realizes an allowed coverage value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Partial-coverage optimization restricts a branching to touch a prescribed number or range of vertices, including exact-coverage and unrestricted nonspanning cases.
knowledge_statements.title: Partial-Coverage Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The bounded-coverage condition is precise and fits the partial-coverage leaf, including its feasibility caveat. Its incidence-based coverage convention and claimed relationship to nonspanning regimes require an inspectable source locator.

children.title: Cardinality–Coverage Interaction
children.top_down_role: Structural interaction between branching size and covered vertex sets.

assumptions_latex: \((U,F)\) is a finite directed branching forest.
Every vertex of \(U\), including an isolated root, is declared covered.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Cardinality, coverage, and root count satisfy \(|F|=|U|-r(F)\).

notation.meaning: Declared covered vertex set.
Number of indegree-zero vertices, equivalently branching components.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: elementary component-count identity for directed branching forests
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coverage includes declared isolated roots, making the cardinality–coverage relation exact.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Each weak component of \((U,F)\) is an out-arborescence and contains exactly one indegree-zero root. Consequently,
\[
|F|=|U|-r(F).
\]
Hence fixing any two of arc cardinality \(|F|\), coverage \(|U|\), and root count \(r(F)\) fixes the third. In particular, among branchings covering exactly \(q\) declared vertices, an exact cardinality constraint \(|F|=k\) is equivalent to requiring exactly \(q-k\) roots, so necessarily \(0\le k\le q-1\) whenever \(q>0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a branching forest, selected arcs equal covered vertices minus roots. Thus cardinality and coverage jointly determine the number of components.
knowledge_statements.title: Cardinality–Coverage Interaction

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The identity |F|=|U|-r(F) is correct for a declared branching forest, and property fits the interaction leaf. However, this record counts declared isolated roots as covered whereas adjacent records use incidence-based coverage, so a source is needed to justify and align the convention before the interaction claim can be relied upon locally.

children.title: Chu–Liu–Edmonds Algorithm Family
children.top_down_role: Contraction-based exact methods for optimum directed spanning structures.

children.title: Cycle Contraction-Expansion Correspondence
children.top_down_role: The recursive structural mechanism of optimum arborescence algorithms.

children.title: Cycle Contraction
children.top_down_role: Compression of directed cycles within optimum-arborescence computation.

assumptions_latex: \(D=(V,A)\) is a finite weighted digraph with root \(r\), and each \(v\ne r\) has a selected minimum-weight incoming arc \(e_v\).
The selected arcs contain a directed cycle \(C\), necessarily excluding \(r\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Contracting \(C\) and reducing each entering-arc weight by the selected weight at its head produces the recursive Chu–Liu–Edmonds instance.

notation.meaning: Supervertex obtained by contracting the cycle.
Selected minimum-weight arc entering vertex v.
Adjusted weight in the contracted instance.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimum-weight rooted out-arborescence convention; parallel arcs created by contraction are retained.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Replace all vertices of \(C\) by one supervertex \(c_C\). Delete arcs internal to \(C\). Map every arc leaving \(C\) to an arc leaving \(c_C\), preserving its weight. Map each arc \(a=(u,v)\) with \(u\notin C\) and \(v\in C\) to an arc \((u,c_C)\) carrying its original head \(v\) and set
\[
w'(u,c_C)=w(a)-w(e_v).
\]
All other arcs and weights remain unchanged. Recursively solve the minimum rooted arborescence problem on the resulting contracted multidigraph.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Contract a selected directed cycle to one supervertex, retain parallel arcs, and subtract the chosen incoming weight at each head from arcs entering the cycle.
knowledge_statements.title: Cycle Contraction

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The contraction rule matches the minimum-cost rooted out-arborescence convention and algorithm is the correct content kind for this leaf. The exact reduced-cost rule and multidigraph handling have no cited source or inspectable algorithm locator.

children.title: Cycle Expansion
children.top_down_role: Recovery of original cycle structure after solving a contracted instance.

assumptions_latex: A cycle \(C\) was contracted using selected internal arcs \(e_v\) for \(v\in C\).
A rooted arborescence \(T'\) of the contracted instance contains an arc entering the supervertex and carrying original head \(v\in C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Replacing the supervertex by \(C\), restoring all \(e_x\) except \(e_v\), and restoring the entering arc yields a rooted arborescence of the uncontracted graph.

notation.meaning: Arborescence in the contracted graph.
Original entering arc represented by the contracted entering arc.
Expanded arborescence.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard inverse expansion step of Chu–Liu–Edmonds contraction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Expansion applies to a nonroot contracted cycle, so the contracted arborescence has one entering arc.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Replace the contracted entering arc in \(T'\) by its represented original arc \(a=(u,v)\). Restore the selected cycle arcs except the one entering \(v\), and retain all other uncontracted representatives of arcs of \(T'\):
\[
T=\bigl(T'\text{ lifted to original arcs}\bigr)\cup\{e_x:x\in C\setminus\{v\}\}.
\]
The omission of \(e_v\) breaks the directed cycle, while \(a\) gives \(v\) its unique incoming arc. Output \(T\) after recursively expanding any remaining supervertices.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Expand a contracted cycle by restoring its chosen cycle arcs except the one entering the head selected by the contracted solution's entering arc.
knowledge_statements.title: Cycle Expansion

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The expansion operation is coherent for a contracted nonroot cycle and algorithm fits the terminal container. The restoration rule and its feasibility claim require an authoritative, specifically located arborescence-algorithm source.

children.title: Contraction–Expansion Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Relationship between contracted solutions and reconstructed arborescences.

assumptions_latex: Cycle contraction uses \(w'(u,c_C)=w(u,v)-w(e_v)\) for every original arc \((u,v)\) entering \(C\).
\(T'\) is a rooted arborescence of the contracted graph and \(T\) is its prescribed expansion.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Contraction and expansion preserve feasibility and shift every corresponding objective value by the constant \(\sum_{x\in C}w(e_x)\).

notation.meaning: Selected incoming arc of a cycle vertex.
Contracted and expanded arborescences.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard constant-shift correspondence underlying cycle contraction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Correspondence is stated for minimum rooted arborescences and a single contracted selected cycle.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Every rooted arborescence \(T'\) of the contracted instance expands, using its unique arc entering \(c_C\), to a rooted arborescence \(T\) of the original instance. Their costs obey
\[
w(T)=w'(T')+\sum_{x\in C}w(e_x).
\]
Conversely, any original rooted arborescence that contains all but one of the selected cycle arcs contracts to the corresponding \(T'\) and satisfies the same identity. Since the added term is independent of \(T'\), minimum-cost contracted solutions expand to minimum-cost solutions within this correspondence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Contracted and expanded arborescences correspond with an objective shift equal to the total weight of the cycle's initially selected incoming arcs.
knowledge_statements.title: Contraction–Expansion Correspondence

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The stated constant-shift identity is consistent with the preceding reduced-cost contraction, and representation is suitable for the correspondence leaf. No source or specific locator supports the feasibility correspondence and objective identity.

children.title: Nested-Cycle Regimes
children.top_down_role: Contraction structure involving multiple or recursively embedded directed cycles.

assumptions_latex: Chu–Liu–Edmonds repeatedly contracts directed cycles in successive quotient graphs.
Each supervertex records the complete preimage of the vertices it represents.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The recorded preimage sets form a laminar family and must be expanded in reverse contraction order.

notation.meaning: Original-vertex preimage represented by a contracted supervertex z.
Family of all recorded contraction preimages.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: quotient contractions produce disjoint-or-contained original-vertex preimages
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nested cycles are cycles in successive quotient graphs, not necessarily simultaneous cycles in the original graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(S_z\subseteq V\) be the original-vertex preimage of every supervertex created during repeated contraction. Then
\[
S_x\cap S_y\in\{\varnothing,S_x,S_y\}
\qquad\text{for all }S_x,S_y\in\mathcal{L}.
\]
Thus \(\mathcal{L}\) is laminar: a later contracted cycle may contain an earlier supervertex, but cannot partially overlap its preimage. Reconstruction expands supervertices in reverse order of contraction; at each expansion, the entering arc identifies which selected internal arc is omitted. This order yields a well-defined arborescence in the original graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeated contractions create disjoint or nested vertex sets. Expanding them in reverse order uniquely propagates each entering-arc choice back to the original graph.
knowledge_statements.title: Nested-Cycle Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The laminar-preimage property and reverse expansion order are plausible and appropriately classified as a property of nested contraction regimes. They lack an inspectable source locator, particularly for the reconstruction assertion.

children.title: Primal-Dual Arborescence Methods
children.top_down_role: Dual-growth interpretations of contraction-based optimization.

assumptions_latex: \(D=(V,A)\) is a finite digraph with root \(r\) from which every vertex is reachable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Dual growth on deficient vertex sets, restricted to dual-feasible tight arcs, gives a primal-dual interpretation of contraction-based minimum-arborescence optimization.

notation.meaning: Arcs entering a vertex subset S.
Nonnegative dual variable for the entering-cut constraint of S.
Primal arc-incidence variable.

review_flags: source_scope_indirect: locator supports general primal-dual methodology but requires arborescence-specific confirmation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cut-LP interpretation for minimum-cost rooted out-arborescences with nonnegative costs.

source_refs.locator: 5.13 Primal-dual methods p. 72

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider the primal cut relaxation
\[
\min\sum_{a\in A}c_ax_a\quad\text{subject to}\quad x(\delta^-(S))\ge1\ \text{for }\varnothing\ne S\subseteq V\setminus\{r\},\quad x\ge0,
\]
with dual
\[
\max\sum_S y_S\quad\text{subject to}\quad\sum_{S:a\in\delta^-(S)}y_S\le c_a\ \text{for }a\in A,
\quad y_S\ge0.
\]
A primal-dual arborescence method raises variables of uncovered sets until entering arcs become tight, selects tight arcs, and contracts tight directed cycles. Expansion recovers a primal arborescence satisfying the complementary tightness conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Primal-dual arborescence methods grow dual cut variables until arcs become tight, contract tight cycles, and later expand them to recover a minimum-cost rooted arborescence.
knowledge_statements.title: Primal-Dual Arborescence Methods

source_witnesses.locator: 5.13 Primal-dual methods p. 72

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The cut primal-dual formulation and principle classification fit the topic, but the cited locator covers general primal-dual methods rather than specifically supporting arborescence dual growth, tight-cycle contraction, expansion, and complementary tightness. An arborescence-specific section or theorem is required.

children.title: Contraction Data-Structure Implementation Family
children.top_down_role: Data-structural refinements of the contraction algorithm family.

children.title: Fast Contraction Implementations
children.top_down_role: Efficient representations for repeated cycle contraction in arborescence optimization.

assumptions_latex: The input is a finite weighted digraph with \(n\) vertices and \(m\) arcs.
Contractions preserve parallel arcs and support lazy uniform key offsets for arcs entering a component.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A contraction implementation with logarithmic-time queue and component operations executes the Chu–Liu–Edmonds recursion in \(O((m+n)\log n)\) time and \(O(m+n)\) space.

notation.meaning: Number of vertices.
Number of arcs.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Comparison-based implementation bound assuming logarithmic amortized meld, deletion, and component operations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Maintain each current contracted component with a meldable queue of candidate entering arcs, a disjoint-set representation of current endpoints, and a contraction forest for later expansion. Discard an extracted arc when its endpoints currently belong to the same component; otherwise process it once as a candidate entering arc. If queue meld, minimum deletion, lazy key adjustment, and component merging each cost \(O(\log n)\) amortized, then at most \(O(m+n)\) such operations are performed. The resulting running time is \(O((m+n)\log n)\), and the stored arcs, queue nodes, and contraction history use \(O(m+n)\) space.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With meldable queues, component merging, and lazy weight offsets, a contraction-based arborescence implementation can run in near-linear logarithmic time and linear space.
knowledge_statements.title: Fast Contraction Implementations

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Complexity bound is the correct role for the claim and fits the fast-implementation leaf. The asserted O(m+n) operation count, amortized data-structure assumptions, O((m+n) log n) running time, and linear-space bound need an authoritative implementation source with an exact locator.

children.title: Meldable-Queue Implementations
children.top_down_role: Priority-queue organizations supporting merges across contracted components.

assumptions_latex: Every current contracted component owns a meldable priority queue of arcs entering it.
Queue keys equal reduced entering-arc costs and support a lazy additive offset.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Melding component queues and lazily adjusting their keys implements contraction without rescanning all incident arcs.

notation.meaning: Priority queue belonging to current component X.
Current contracted component containing vertex v.
Reduced-cost key of an arc.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard meldable-heap organization for contraction algorithms
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Abstract data-structure formulation; the concrete heap and amortized bounds are left implementation-dependent.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Initialize \(Q_{\{v\}}\) with all arcs entering \(v\), keyed by \(\kappa(a)=w(a)\). To select an entering arc for a component \(X\), repeatedly delete a minimum-key arc \((u,v)\) until \(\operatorname{comp}(u)\ne X\). When selected arcs form a directed cycle with components \(X_1,\ldots,X_t\), create \(X=\bigcup_iX_i\), apply to each \(Q_{X_i}\) the lazy key offset prescribed by reduced-cost contraction, and set
\[
Q_X=\operatorname{meld}(Q_{X_1},\ldots,Q_{X_t}).
\]
Retain provenance pointers for reverse-order expansion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each contracted component keeps a meldable queue of entering arcs. Lazy offsets and queue melding perform reduced-cost contraction without rebuilding all queues.
knowledge_statements.title: Meldable-Queue Implementations

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The meldable-queue organization is relevant to the exact leaf and algorithm is an appropriate content kind. The lazy offsets are referenced but not explicitly defined, and no authoritative source with a specific locator supports the queue invariant, stale-arc deletion, melding, and provenance scheme.

children.title: Component-Merge Data Structures
children.top_down_role: Structures maintaining component state during recursive contractions.

assumptions_latex: A finite directed multigraph \(D=(V,A)\) is given.
Each current contracted component owns a meldable queue of arcs entering it.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The maintained partition and queues implement every contraction while preserving the minimum reduced-cost entering arc of each current component.

notation.meaning: current contracted component containing a vertex
queue associated with component C

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Abstract disjoint-set and meldable-queue interface for Chu–Liu–Edmonds contractions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize one disjoint-set component \(C_v=\{v\}\) and one entering-arc queue \(Q_{C_v}\) for each \(v\in V\). Support \(\operatorname{Find}(v)\), \(\operatorname{Merge}(C_1,C_2)\), and \(\operatorname{Meld}(Q_{C_1},Q_{C_2})\). When a directed cycle of selected entering arcs is found, merge all its components and meld their queues. Repeatedly delete from the resulting queue every arc \(uv\) with \(\operatorname{Find}(u)=\operatorname{Find}(v)\); the first remaining minimum-key arc is the minimum reduced-cost arc entering the contracted component. Store the contraction forest and selected arcs so that contractions can be expanded in reverse order to recover the arborescence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Disjoint sets represent contracted cycles, while meldable queues combine their entering arcs and discard newly internal arcs; a contraction forest supports final expansion.
knowledge_statements.title: Component-Merge Data Structures

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm content kind fits the implementation leaf, but no citation is supplied. The claim that melding queues and deleting internal arcs preserves the minimum reduced-cost entering arc depends on an unspecified reduced-cost key-update or lazy-offset invariant, and the expansion bookkeeping also requires exact implementation support.

children.title: Implementation Complexity Regimes
children.top_down_role: Running-time behavior under different contraction and queue representations.

assumptions_latex: The input digraph has \(n=|V|\) vertices and \(m=|A|\) arcs.
Heap keys support the reduced-cost adjustments required during contractions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A standard heap-and-component implementation uses \(O(m\log n)\) time and \(O(m+n)\) space; simpler repeated scanning can require \(O(mn)\) time.

notation.meaning: number of vertices
number of arcs

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Comparison of scanning and meldable-heap implementations of directed cycle contraction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a Chu–Liu–Edmonds implementation that contracts each discovered directed cycle, repeated rescanning of all arcs after contractions gives the coarse bound \(O(mn)\). If contracted components are maintained by disjoint sets and their entering arcs by meldable heaps, each arc is inserted once, discarded at most once after becoming internal, and participates in \(O(\log n)\)-amortized priority-queue work. Under this comparison-based implementation model, the total running time is \(O(m\log n)\) and the storage is \(O(m+n)\). More specialized contraction structures may improve this regime, so the bound is implementation-specific rather than a universal lower bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeated arc scans give a coarse quadratic-factor regime; disjoint sets and meldable heaps yield a standard near-linear, logarithmic-factor implementation.
knowledge_statements.title: Implementation Complexity Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The complexity_bound kind fits the exact leaf, but the stated O(m log n) time and O(m+n) space require a source identifying the heap type, reduced-cost update mechanism, component operations, and amortization argument. The assertion that every arc incurs only O(log n)-amortized queue work is not established by the supplied record.

children.title: Directed Spanning Min-Max Duality Family
children.top_down_role: Dual characterization families for optimum directed spanning and forest structures.

children.title: Shortest-Arborescence Min-Max Family
children.top_down_role: Dual characterization family for optimum rooted arborescences.

assumptions_latex: \(D=(V,A)\) is a finite digraph with root \(r\in V\).
Every vertex is reachable from \(r\), and arc costs \(c_a\in\mathbb{R}\) are finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The minimum cost of an \(r\)-arborescence equals the maximum weight of a feasible packing of nonempty root-avoiding entering-cut demands.

notation.meaning: arcs entering a vertex set S
nonnegative dual variable for an entering-cut constraint

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cut-packing duality for minimum-cost spanning out-arborescences rooted at \(r\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mathcal{S}=\{S:\varnothing\ne S\subseteq V\setminus\{r\}\}\). Then
\[
\min\left\{\sum_{a\in A}c_ax_a:x\ge0,\ \sum_{a\in\delta^-(S)}x_a\ge1\ \text{for every }S\in\mathcal{S}\right\}
=
\max\left\{\sum_{S\in\mathcal{S}}y_S:y\ge0,\ \sum_{S\in\mathcal{S}:a\in\delta^-(S)}y_S\le c_a\ \text{for every }a\in A\right\}.
\]
The integral optimum vectors on the primal side are incidence vectors of spanning out-arborescences rooted at \(r\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Minimum rooted-arborescence cost equals the maximum feasible packing of root-avoiding entering cuts, with each arc paying for all cuts it enters.
knowledge_statements.title: Shortest-Arborescence Min-Max Family

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The duality kind fits the min-max family, but the formula is not reliable under the stated arbitrary real costs: the cut-covering primal can exploit negative-cost arcs and the displayed nonnegative packing dual may be infeasible. Moreover, the assertion that integral optimum vectors are arborescence incidence vectors is too strong for the dominant cut formulation; at most an arborescence optimum may exist under suitable cost assumptions. An exact arborescence-duality source and corrected hypotheses are required.

children.title: Longest-Branching Min-Max Family
children.top_down_role: Dual characterization family for optimum variable-root branchings.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The maximum weight of a branching equals the minimum value of the displayed vertex-and-subset covering dual.

notation.meaning: arcs with both endpoints in S
head vertex of arc a
nonnegative vertex and subset dual variables

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear-programming min-max formula for maximum-weight variable-root branchings.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The maximum-weight branching value is
\[
\max\left\{\sum_{a\in A}w_ax_a:x\ge0,\ x(\delta^-(v))\le1\ (v\in V),\ x(A[S])\le |S|-1\ (\varnothing\ne S\subseteq V)\right\}.
\]
By branching-polytope integrality, this equals
\[
\min\left\{\sum_{v\in V}p_v+\sum_{\varnothing\ne S\subseteq V}(|S|-1)q_S:p,q\ge0,\ p_{h(a)}+\sum_{S:a\in A[S]}q_S\ge w_a\ (a\in A)\right\}.
\]
Thus the dual covers every arc weight by a head-vertex price and prices of vertex sets containing both endpoints.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Maximum branching weight equals a minimum dual cover using vertex prices and prices on induced vertex subsets.
knowledge_statements.title: Longest-Branching Min-Max Family

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The duality kind matches the variable-root branching min-max container, and the primal-dual pair is plausible. No cited source supports the branching-polytope description, its integrality, or this exact weighted dual formula, so the mathematical version cannot be admitted without an inspectable theorem or section locator.

children.title: Laminar Uncrossing Certificate System
children.top_down_role: Structured dual certificates for directed spanning optimization.

children.title: Tight-Cut Uncrossing
children.top_down_role: Structural simplification of intersecting tight directed cuts.

assumptions_latex: The sets \(A,B\subseteq V\setminus\{r\}\) cross and satisfy \(x(\delta^-(A))=x(\delta^-(B))=1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Both \(A\cap B\) and \(A\cup B\) are tight, and equality holds in the directed in-cut submodularity inequality.

notation.meaning: arcs entering S from its complement
sum of x over an arc set F

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uncrossing of tight root-avoiding entering cuts.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Directed in-cuts satisfy
\[
x(\delta^-(A))+x(\delta^-(B))\ge x(\delta^-(A\cap B))+x(\delta^-(A\cup B)).
\]
Because crossing implies \(A\cap B\ne\varnothing\), and because both derived sets avoid \(r\), primal feasibility makes each term on the right at least \(1\). Tightness of \(A\) and \(B\) makes the left side equal to \(2\). Consequently
\[
x(\delta^-(A\cap B))=x(\delta^-(A\cup B))=1,
\]
so intersection and union preserve tightness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two crossing tight entering cuts can be replaced by their intersection and union, which are also tight.
knowledge_statements.title: Tight-Cut Uncrossing

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property kind is suitable for tight-cut uncrossing, and the stated intersection-union conclusion is standard under the given feasibility assumptions. However, no directed-cut uncrossing source is cited, and the statement includes a proof-style derivation beginning with primal feasibility and concluding tightness, contrary to the no-proof requirement. A sourced, proof-free formulation is needed.

children.title: Laminar Dual Families
children.top_down_role: Nested organization of cut sets supporting optimum directed spanning certificates.

assumptions_latex: The rooted arborescence cut linear program is feasible and has finite optimum.
Its arc costs permit a feasible dual.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There exists an optimal dual solution whose positive-support family is laminar.

notation.meaning: support of the dual vector
a laminar family of vertex sets

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Existence, not uniqueness, of a laminar optimum for the rooted cut-packing dual.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Among all optimal solutions of the dual
\[
\max\left\{\sum_{\varnothing\ne S\subseteq V\setminus\{r\}}y_S:y\ge0,\ \sum_{S:a\in\delta^-(S)}y_S\le c_a\ (a\in A)\right\},
\]
there is a solution \(y^*\) for which \(\operatorname{supp}(y^*)\) is laminar: for any \(A,B\in\operatorname{supp}(y^*)\), either \(A\subseteq B\), \(B\subseteq A\), or \(A\cap B=\varnothing\). The assertion is existential; other optimal dual solutions may have crossing positive-support sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The rooted arborescence dual always has an optimal solution supported on a laminar family, although nonlaminar optima may also exist.
knowledge_statements.title: Laminar Dual Families

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem kind fits the existential laminar-optimum leaf, and the distinction between existence and uniqueness is appropriate. No source is supplied for the exact rooted cut-packing dual or for the existence of an optimal laminar support under the stated hypotheses.

children.title: Uncrossing–Laminarity Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Relationship between cut simplification and laminar dual support.

assumptions_latex: The dual set system is closed under union and nonempty intersection of crossing members.
The cut coefficient function admits the standard uncrossing replacement without violating arc constraints.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Repeated objective-preserving uncrossing terminates at a laminar optimal support, while every laminar optimum is already uncrossed.

notation.meaning: uncrossing step size
dual variable indexed by S

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalence between exhausted crossing-pair replacements and laminar dual support.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If crossing sets \(A,B\) have \(y_A,y_B>0\), set \(\varepsilon=\min\{y_A,y_B\}\), decrease \(y_A,y_B\) by \(\varepsilon\), and increase \(y_{A\cap B},y_{A\cup B}\) by \(\varepsilon\). For the rooted arborescence cut dual, this replacement preserves the objective and dual feasibility. Choosing uncrossing steps according to a strictly improving finite set-family potential yields an optimal dual with no crossing support pairs, hence laminar support. Conversely, a laminar support contains no eligible crossing pair and is a fixed point of this uncrossing operation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Objective-preserving replacements of crossing sets by intersection and union lead exactly to dual supports with no crossings, namely laminar families.
knowledge_statements.title: Uncrossing–Laminarity Correspondence

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The principle kind fits the correspondence leaf, but feasibility preservation and finite termination require a precise uncrossing theorem and a specified strictly improving potential. The converse fixed-point observation is valid for the stated operation, but it does not supply evidence for the forward termination claim.

children.title: Nonlaminar Certificate Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Dual configurations requiring care before laminar organization is available.

assumptions_latex: The digraph contains all arcs needed by the displayed dual constraints, with costs defined from the dual vector below.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Laminarity is not necessary for an optimal certificate: the constructed optimal dual has crossing support.

notation.meaning: two crossing root-avoiding sets
dual cut-packing vector

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary: uncrossing proves existence of laminar optima, not laminarity of every optimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Set \(y_{A_0}=y_{B_0}=1\) and all other dual variables to \(0\). Assign each arc \(e\) the cost
\[
c_e=\mathbf{1}[e\in\delta^-(A_0)]+\mathbf{1}[e\in\delta^-(B_0)].
\]
Then \(y\) is dual feasible with value \(2\). The arcs \(ra,ab,bc\) form an \(r\)-arborescence of cost \(1+1+0=2\), so weak duality makes both solutions optimal. Since \(A_0\cap B_0=\{b\}\) and neither set contains the other, the optimal dual certificate is nonlaminar. Thus laminarization is a permissible normalization, not a necessary property of every certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A four-vertex instance has an optimal dual supported on two crossing sets, showing that optimal certificates need not themselves be laminar.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonlaminar Certificate Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure_boundary kind is exactly appropriate, and the displayed crossing-support construction is internally plausible. Nevertheless, the digraph is described only as containing arcs needed by unspecified constraints, rather than being defined exactly, and no source or registered independent-verification evidence supports the counterexample.

children.title: Branching Polytope

assumptions_latex: A branching is an arc set whose indegrees are at most one and whose underlying undirected graph is acyclic.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Edmonds' inequality description for the unrestricted directed branching polytope.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The branching polytope of \(D\) is
\[
P_B(D)=\operatorname{conv}\{\chi^F:F\subseteq A\text{ is a branching}\}.
\]
It has the linear description
\[
P_B(D)=\left\{x\in\mathbb{R}_{\ge0}^{A}:x(\delta^-(v))\le1\ \text{for every }v\in V,\quad x(A[S])\le |S|-1\ \text{for every nonempty }S\subseteq V\right\}.
\]
The singleton subset inequalities are redundant, but retaining them gives a uniform family.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The branching polytope is defined by nonnegativity, at most one entering arc per vertex, and forest inequalities on every vertex subset.
knowledge_statements.title: Branching Polytope

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation kind fits the Branching Polytope container, and the inequality system is the standard candidate description. knowledge_statements.statement_title: Linear description of the branching polytope
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Complete inequality description of the convex hull of incidence vectors of branchings in a digraph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a digraph \(D=(V,A)\), let \(A(W)\) be the set of arcs having both endpoints in \(W\). Then
\[\operatorname{conv}\{\chi^B\in\mathbb R^A:B\subseteq A\text{ is a branching}\}=\{x\in\mathbb R^A:x(\delta^-(v))\le 1\ \forall v\in V,\ x(A(W))\le |W|-1\ \forall\varnothing\ne W\subseteq V,\ x_a\ge 0\ \forall a\in A\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The branching polytope consists exactly of the nonnegative arc vectors having entering-arc sum at most one at every vertex and internal-arc sum at most |W|−1 for every nonempty vertex subset W.
assumptions_latex: A(W)=\{a\in A:\text{both endpoints of }a\text{ lie in }W\}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{conv}\{\chi^B:B\text{ is a branching}\}=\{x\ge 0:x(\delta^-(v))\le 1\ \forall v\in V,\ x(A(W))\le |W|-1\ \forall\varnothing\ne W\subseteq V\}.

children.title: Rooted Arborescence Polytope
children.top_down_role: The polyhedral model for root-prescribed directed spanning structures.

assumptions_latex: \(D=(V,A)\) is a finite digraph and \(r\in V\).
Every vertex of \(V\setminus\{r\}\) is reachable from \(r\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed cut system is the convex hull of incidence vectors of spanning out-arborescences rooted at \(r\).

notation.meaning: arcs entering S from V minus S
rooted arborescence polytope

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cut description for spanning out-arborescences with prescribed root.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mathcal{A}_r\) be the family of spanning out-arborescences rooted at \(r\). Then
\[
P_r(D)=\operatorname{conv}\{\chi^T:T\in\mathcal{A}_r\}
\]
is described by
\[
P_r(D)=\left\{x\in\mathbb{R}_{\ge0}^{A}:x(\delta^-(r))=0,\ x(\delta^-(v))=1\ \text{for every }v\ne r,\ x(\delta^-(S))\ge1\ \text{for every }\varnothing\ne S\subseteq V\setminus\{r\}\right\}.
\]
Equivalently, the vertex equalities may be replaced by \(x(A)=|V|-1\) together with the entering-cut constraints and exclusion of arcs entering \(r\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Rooted arborescences are exactly the integral points satisfying one incoming arc per nonroot vertex and every nonempty root-avoiding entering-cut constraint.
knowledge_statements.title: Rooted Arborescence Polytope

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation kind fits the rooted-arborescence polytope leaf, and the displayed cut system is plausible. It lacks an exact source. In addition, the plain statement says rooted arborescences are exactly the integral points, although an integral polytope contains nonvertex integral points only if permitted by the bounded system; the intended claim should be stated explicitly as a convex-hull or vertex characterization consistent with the LaTeX.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Rooted arborescence polytope and its up hull
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the rooted arborescence polytope and its dominant; the separate inequality descriptions are retained in the associated corollary items.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a digraph $D=(V,A)$ and $r\in V$,
\[
P_{r\text{-arborescence}}(D):=\operatorname{conv}\{\chi^B\in\mathbb R^A:B\text{ is an }r\text{-arborescence}\},
\qquad
P_{r\text{-arborescence}}^{\uparrow}(D):=P_{r\text{-arborescence}}(D)+\mathbb R_+^A.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The r-arborescence polytope is the convex hull of the incidence vectors of all r-arborescences. Its up hull is obtained by adding the nonnegative orthant.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Integral Optimum of the Rooted-Arborescence Cut LP
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Existence and structure of an integral optimum for the nonnegative cut-covering formulation with nonnegative real arc weights.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G\) be a digraph, let \(c:E(G)\to\mathbb R_+\), and let \(r\in V(G)\). Suppose that \(G\) contains a spanning arborescence rooted at \(r\). Then
\[
\min\left\{c^\top x:x\ge0,\ \sum_{e\in\delta^+(X)}x_e\ge1\ \text{for every }X\subsetneq V(G)\text{ with }r\in X\right\}
\]
has an integral optimum. Such an optimum is the incidence vector of a minimum-weight spanning arborescence rooted at \(r\), possibly augmented by zero-weight edges.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If a digraph has a spanning arborescence rooted at r, then its nonnegative outgoing-cut covering LP has an integral optimum; that optimum consists of a minimum-weight rooted spanning arborescence and possibly additional zero-weight arcs.
assumptions_latex: G\text{ contains a spanning arborescence rooted at }r
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The rooted cut-covering LP has an integral optimum equal to a minimum-weight rooted arborescence incidence vector, possibly plus zero-weight arcs.}

children.title: Branching-Polytope Integrality
children.top_down_role: Integral vertex structure of branching formulations.

assumptions_latex: \(P_B(D)\) is defined by nonnegativity, indegree inequalities, and induced-subgraph forest inequalities.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every vertex of \(P_B(D)\) is a zero-one incidence vector of a branching.

notation.meaning: branching polytope of D

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Integrality of Edmonds' unrestricted branching-polytope description.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For
\[
P_B(D)=\left\{x\in\mathbb{R}_{\ge0}^{A}:x(\delta^-(v))\le1\ (v\in V),\ x(A[S])\le |S|-1\ (\varnothing\ne S\subseteq V)\right\},
\]
every extreme point is integral. More precisely,
\[
\operatorname{vert}(P_B(D))\subseteq\{\chi^F:F\subseteq A\text{ is a branching}\}.
\]
Consequently, for every rational weight vector \(w\), if \(\max\{w^{\mathsf T}x:x\in P_B(D)\}\) is finite, it has an optimal branching incidence vector.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every extreme point of the branching inequality system is a branching incidence vector, so linear optimization admits an integral optimum.
knowledge_statements.title: Branching-Polytope Integrality

children.title: Total Dual Integrality
children.top_down_role: Dual-integrality structure associated with directed spanning formulations.

assumptions_latex: The branching inequality system is written with an integral right-hand side.
The dual linear program has a finite optimum for the integral objective under consideration.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The branching system is totally dual integral; hence every integral objective with finite dual optimum has an integral optimal dual solution.

notation.meaning: constraint matrix and right-hand side of the branching system

knowledge_statements.scope_note: TDI formulation of the indegree and induced-subgraph branching inequalities.

source_refs.locator: Section 5.3. Total Dual Integrality p. 111
5.17 Total dual integrality p. 76

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Write the nonnegativity, indegree, and induced-subgraph inequalities defining the branching polytope as \(Mx\le b\), after reversing signs where necessary. This system is totally dual integral: for every \(w\in\mathbb{Z}^{A}\) such that
\[
\max\{w^{\mathsf T}x:Mx\le b\}
\]
has a finite optimum, the dual
\[
\min\{b^{\mathsf T}y:M^{\mathsf T}y=w,\ y\ge0\}
\]
has an integral optimal solution. Since \(b\) is integral, total dual integrality also implies integrality of the resulting branching polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The branching inequality system has integral optimal dual multipliers for every integral objective, and its integral right-hand side yields an integral polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.title: Total Dual Integrality

source_witnesses.locator: Section 5.3. Total Dual Integrality p. 111
5.17 Total dual integrality p. 76

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property kind fits the Total Dual Integrality leaf, and both citations have specific locators, but those locators identify generic TDI sections rather than a theorem establishing that this particular branching inequality system is TDI. A branching-specific theorem or an exact locator within a source treating the branching system is required; generic TDI definitions alone do not support the application.

children.title: Integral Optimum Consequences

knowledge_statements.title: Integral Optimum Consequences
knowledge_statements.scope_note: TDI consequence for the rooted branching-forest linear program.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D=(V,A)\), let \(R\subseteq V\) be a nonempty root set, and let \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{A}\) be the polyhedron defined by nonnegativity, zero indegree at roots, unit indegree at nonroots, and \(x(\delta^-(S))\ge 1\) for every nonempty \(S\subseteq V\setminus R\). If this defining system is totally dual integral, then its integral right-hand side makes \(P\) integral. Consequently, for every \(c\in\mathbb{R}^{A}\) for which \(\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:x\in P\}\) is finite, an optimum is attained at \(x^*=\chi^F\), where \(F\) is a spanning branching forest rooted in \(R\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Total dual integrality makes the branching-forest polyhedron integral, so every finite linear optimization problem over it has an optimal branching-forest incidence vector.
assumptions_latex: \(D=(V,A)\) is a finite digraph and \(\varnothing\ne R\subseteq V\).
The displayed branching system is totally dual integral.
The linear objective has a finite optimum over \(P\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There exists an optimal solution \(x^*=\chi^F\) for a spanning branching forest \(F\) rooted in \(R\).

rooted branching-forest polyhedron

children.title: Integrality Failure Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Formulation changes or side constraints that can disrupt integral structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Integrality Failure Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A linear side constraint can destroy branching-polytope integrality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(V=\{r,u,v\}\) and \(A=\{ru,rv,uv,vu\}\). The rooted-arborescence polytope is \[P=\{x\ge0:x_{ru}+x_{vu}=1,\ x_{rv}+x_{uv}=1,\ x_{ru}+x_{rv}\ge1\}.\] It is integral. Intersecting it with the side constraint \(x_{ru}=x_{rv}\) produces the fractional vertex \[x_{ru}=x_{rv}=x_{uv}=x_{vu}=\tfrac12.\] Indeed, both indegree equations, the side constraint, and the tight cut equation \(x_{ru}+x_{rv}=1\) uniquely determine this point. Thus integrality of the branching polytope is not preserved under arbitrary linear side constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Even one additional equality can create a fractional vertex in an otherwise integral rooted-arborescence polytope.
assumptions_latex: \(D\) has the displayed three vertices and four arcs.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The intersection \(P\cap\{x:x_{ru}=x_{rv}\}\) is not integral.

notation.meaning: rooted-arborescence polytope of the displayed digraph
selection coordinate of arc a

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The displayed intersection does have the claimed fractional vertex and fits a failure-boundary container, but the exact counterexample has no cited source.

children.title: Compact Formulations

knowledge_statements.title: Compact Formulations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Direct polynomial-size descriptions in the original arc space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D=(V,A)\) be a finite digraph, let \(R\subseteq V\) be a nonempty root set, and let \(P(D,R)\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{A}\) be its branching polytope. A compact formulation in the original arc space is a rational system \(B(D,R)x\le d(D,R)\) such that \[P(D,R)=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^{A}:B(D,R)x\le d(D,R)\}\] and whose total binary encoding length is bounded by a polynomial in \(|V|+|A|\). Thus an exponentially indexed cut description is not compact in this sense, even if its inequalities admit polynomial-time separation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A compact formulation is an exact rational description of the branching polytope in the original arc variables whose total encoding size is polynomial in the digraph size.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(B(D,R)x\le d(D,R)\) is compact precisely when it describes \(P(D,R)\) exactly in the original arc space and has polynomial total binary encoding length.

notation.meaning: branching polytope for digraph D and root set R

knowledge_statements.title: Extended Formulations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Branching-polytope descriptions with auxiliary variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{A}\) be a rational branching polytope. An extended formulation of \(P\) consists of integers \(k,m\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge0}\) and rational data \(E\in\mathbb{Q}^{m\times A}\), \(F\in\mathbb{Q}^{m\times k}\), and \(g\in\mathbb{Q}^{m}\) defining \[Q=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb{R}^{A}\times\mathbb{R}^{k}:Ex+Fy\le g\}\] such that \[P=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^{A}:\exists y\in\mathbb{R}^{k},\ (x,y)\in Q\}.\] Its size is conventionally measured by its number of inequalities, with coefficient encoding length also included when computational input size is relevant. The auxiliary coordinates may encode flows, potentials, orders, or other certificates and need not be branching-incidence coordinates.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An extended formulation describes a rational higher-dimensional polyhedron whose projection onto the original arc variables is exactly the branching polytope.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Q\) is an extended formulation of \(P\) exactly when its projection onto the \(x\)-coordinates equals \(P\).

notation.meaning: higher-dimensional formulation polyhedron
auxiliary-variable vector

children.title: Projection Correspondence

knowledge_statements.title: Projection Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact correspondence between an extension and its arc-space projection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{A}\times\mathbb{R}^{k}\) be an extended formulation of \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{A}\), and let \(\pi(x,y)=x\). Then \(\pi(Q)=P\). Hence, for every \(c\in\mathbb{R}^{A}\), \[\inf_{x\in P}c^{\mathsf T}x=\inf_{(x,y)\in Q}c^{\mathsf T}x.\] Moreover, every feasible \((x,y)\in Q\) projects to an arc-space feasible point, and every \(x\in P\) has at least one lift \(y\) with \((x,y)\in Q\). If optima are attained, projection and lifting preserve optimal objective values.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Projection maps every extended feasible point to the branching polytope, every branching point has a lift, and arc-based optimization values agree.
assumptions_latex: \(Q\) is an exact extended formulation of \(P\).
The objective depends only on the arc variables \(x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\pi(Q)=P\) and \(\inf_{x\in P}c^{\mathsf T}x=\inf_{(x,y)\in Q}c^{\mathsf T}x\).

knowledge_statements.title: Formulation-Size Tradeoffs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit cut count versus polynomial-time separation for rooted arborescences.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a rooted digraph \(D=(V,A)\) with root \(r\), the standard arc-space description contains the inequalities \(x(\delta^-(S))\ge1\) for all nonempty \(S\subseteq V\setminus\{r\}\), hence has \(2^{|V|-1}-1\) indexed cut inequalities before redundancy removal. Given a candidate \(x\ge0\), a violated cut exists exactly when some minimum \(r\)-to-\(v\) cut, using capacities \(x_a\), has value below \(1\). Thus the formulation may be exponentially large explicitly while possessing polynomial-time separation; an extension can trade auxiliary variables for fewer explicit inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The rooted cut formulation has exponentially many indexed inequalities, but minimum-cut computations separate them in polynomial time; extensions may exchange variables for rows.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The cut family is exponentially indexed but polynomial-time separable by minimum \(r\)-to-\(v\) cuts.

knowledge_statements.title: Root-Reachability Obstructions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Directed-cut certificate for failure of a rooted spanning out-arborescence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D=(V,A)\) be a finite digraph with prescribed root \(r\in V\). A nonempty set \(S\subseteq V\setminus\{r\}\) satisfying \(\delta^-(S)=\varnothing\) is a certificate that no spanning out-arborescence rooted at \(r\) exists. Conversely, a spanning out-arborescence rooted at \(r\) exists if and only if \(\delta^-(S)\ne\varnothing\) for every nonempty \(S\subseteq V\setminus\{r\}\).

knowledge_statements.title: Cycle-Induced Choice Obstructions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Why independent minimum incoming-arc choices need not form an arborescence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Selecting one entering arc independently for each nonroot vertex does not ensure rooted feasibility. For \(V=\{r,u,v\}\) with arcs \(ru,rv,uv,vu\), the local choices \(vu\) for \(u\) and \(uv\) for \(v\) satisfy both unit-indegree requirements but form a directed cycle disjoint from \(r\). More generally, a set \(F\subseteq A\) with \(d_F^-(r)=0\) and \(d_F^-(v)=1\) for every \(v\ne r\) is a rooted spanning out-arborescence exactly when it contains no directed cycle and every vertex is reachable from \(r\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: One incoming arc per nonroot can create a root-disconnected directed cycle, so local choices require global acyclicity and reachability checks.
assumptions_latex: \(F\subseteq A\) gives every nonroot exactly one entering arc and gives \(r\) none.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The indegree choices form a rooted out-arborescence if and only if they contain no directed cycle and reach every vertex from \(r\).

notation.meaning: indegree of v in selected arc set F
set of independently selected arcs

children.title: Degree-Constrained Arborescences
children.top_down_role: Rooted directed spanning structures subject to vertex-degree restrictions.

knowledge_statements.title: Degree-Constrained Arborescences
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hardness boundary created by vertex outdegree caps.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a digraph \(D=(V,A)\), a root \(r\), and upper bounds \(b_v\), the degree-constrained arborescence feasibility problem asks for a spanning out-arborescence \(T\) rooted at \(r\) satisfying \(d_T^+(v)\le b_v\) for every \(v\in V\). When \(b_v=1\) for every vertex, any feasible \(T\) has \(|V|-1\) arcs, no branching vertex, and therefore is a directed Hamiltonian path beginning at \(r\). Conversely, every such Hamiltonian path is feasible. Hence this restricted feasibility problem is NP-complete, assuming the standard NP-completeness of fixed-start directed Hamiltonian path.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Outdegree-one rooted arborescences are exactly directed Hamiltonian paths from the root, making degree-constrained feasibility NP-complete.
assumptions_latex: \(D=(V,A)\) is a finite digraph with prescribed root \(r\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Degree-constrained spanning out-arborescence feasibility is NP-complete even under uniform outdegree bound \(1\).

notation.meaning: outdegree of v in arborescence T
outdegree upper bound at v

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The reduction to fixed-start directed Hamiltonian path is mathematically plausible and the complexity content kind fits, but the NP-completeness premise and claimed restricted hardness have no source locator.

children.title: Hop-Constrained Arborescences
children.top_down_role: Rooted directed spanning structures subject to root-distance limits.

knowledge_statements.title: Hop-Constrained Arborescences
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rooted arborescences with bounded root-to-vertex path length.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D=(V,A)\), let \(r\in V\), and let \(H\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge0}\). An \(H\)-hop-constrained spanning out-arborescence is a spanning out-arborescence \(T\subseteq A\) rooted at \(r\) such that the unique directed path \(P_T(r,v)\) satisfies \[|P_T(r,v)|\le H\qquad\text{for every }v\in V.\] Equivalently, the depth of \(T\) from \(r\) is at most \(H\). The constraint is global: whether an entering arc is admissible depends on the depth induced by all predecessor choices, not solely on that arc.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A hop-constrained arborescence limits every unique root-to-vertex path to at most H arcs, coupling each local parent choice to global depth.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T\) is \(H\)-hop-constrained exactly when \(\max_{v\in V}|P_T(r,v)|\le H\).

notation.meaning: unique directed r-to-v path in T
maximum permitted number of arcs on a root path
spanning out-arborescence

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition is internally precise and distinguishes the global depth variant, but no authoritative source with a locator supports the selected hop-constrained convention.

children.title: Resource-Constrained Arborescences
children.top_down_role: Rooted directed spanning structures subject to budgets or resource capacities.

knowledge_statements.title: Resource-Constrained Arborescences
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global additive-resource version of constrained rooted arborescences.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let each arc \(a\in A\) consume a nonnegative resource vector \(q_a\in\mathbb{R}_{\ge0}^{p}\), and let \(B\in\mathbb{R}_{\ge0}^{p}\). A globally resource-constrained spanning out-arborescence is a spanning out-arborescence \(T\) rooted at \(r\) satisfying \[\sum_{a\in T}q_a\le B,\] where the inequality is componentwise. In incidence variables this predicate is \(\sum_{a\in A}q_a x_a\le B\) together with the rooted-arborescence constraints and \(x\in\{0,1\}^{A}\). This definition selects global budgets; pathwise root-to-vertex resource bounds constitute a distinct variant.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A globally resource-constrained arborescence must respect one or more additive budgets over all selected arcs; pathwise budgets are a separate variant.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Feasibility requires \(T\) to be a rooted spanning out-arborescence and \(\sum_{a\in T}q_a\le B\).

notation.meaning: nonnegative resource-consumption vector of arc a
componentwise global resource budget
binary arc-incidence vector

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The global additive-budget definition is coherent and explicitly separated from pathwise variants, but the selected resource-constrained convention lacks an authoritative source locator.

children.title: Combined-Constraint Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Model behavior when multiple arborescence side constraints are imposed simultaneously.

knowledge_statements.title: Combined-Constraint Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Complexity inheritance when degree, hop, and resource restrictions are combined.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider feasibility of a rooted spanning out-arborescence subject simultaneously to outdegree bounds \(d_T^+(v)\le b_v\), hop bound \(\max_v|P_T(r,v)|\le H\), and global resource bounds \(\sum_{a\in T}q_a\le B\). This combined family contains the degree-constrained family as the special case \(H=|V|-1\), \(q_a=0\) for every \(a\), and \(B=0\). With \(b_v=1\) for every \(v\), feasibility is therefore equivalent to a directed Hamiltonian path beginning at \(r\). Consequently, the combined feasibility problem is NP-complete, even when its hop and resource constraints are nonbinding.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The combined family remains NP-complete because nonbinding hop and resource limits leave the NP-complete outdegree-one arborescence problem as a special case.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Combined degree-, hop-, and resource-constrained arborescence feasibility is NP-complete.

notation.meaning: outdegree upper bound at v
root-path hop bound
arc resource vectors and global budget

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The special-case inheritance argument is coherent and failure_boundary fits the container, but the NP-completeness conclusion depends on the unsourced degree-constrained hardness premise.

knowledge_statements.title: Shortest R–S Biconnectors
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cut formulation of the minimum-weight directed two-sided connector problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D=(V,A)\), let \(R,S\subseteq V\) be disjoint and nonempty, and let \(w\in\mathbb R_+^A\). An \(R\)–\(S\) biconnector is an arc set \(B\subseteq A\) such that every vertex of \(R\) reaches some vertex of \(S\) in \((V,B)\), and every vertex of \(S\) is reachable from some vertex of \(R\). Equivalently, its incidence vector satisfies \(x(\delta^+(X))\ge1\) whenever \(X\cap R\ne\varnothing\) and \(X\cap S=\varnothing\), and \(x(\delta^-(X))\ge1\) whenever \(X\cap S\ne\varnothing\) and \(X\cap R=\varnothing\). The shortest-biconnector value is \[\min\{w^\top x:x\in\{0,1\}^A\text{ satisfies these inequalities}\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose minimum-weight arcs so every root reaches the opposite side and every opposite-side terminal is reachable from a root.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{opt}_{RS}(D,w)=\min\{w^\top x:x\text{ is the incidence vector of an }R\text{–}S\text{ biconnector}\}.\)

notation.meaning: arcs leaving and entering X, respectively

knowledge_statements.title: Longest R–S Biforests
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weighted maximization over the standard directed biforest family.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D=(V,A)\), let \(R,S\subseteq V\) be disjoint and nonempty, and let \(c\in\mathbb R^A\). Denote by \(\mathcal F_{R,S}(D)\) the family of \(R\)–\(S\) biforests in \(D\), in the standard two-sided directed-forest sense. The longest-biforest problem is the finite set optimization problem \[\max\{c(F):F\in\mathcal F_{R,S}(D)\},\qquad c(F):=\sum_{a\in F}c_a.\] An optimizer is any \(F^\star\in\mathcal F_{R,S}(D)\) attaining this maximum. The exact independence axioms defining \(\mathcal F_{R,S}(D)\) require confirmation from the cited source before promotion.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F^\star\in\operatorname*{argmax}_{F\in\mathcal F_{R,S}(D)}c(F).\)

knowledge_statements.title: Minimum-Size Bibranchings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cardinality minimization using the standard two-sided reachability cuts.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D=(V,A)\) have a bipartition \(V=S\mathbin{\dot\cup}T\) with both classes nonempty. A bibranching is an arc set \(B\subseteq A\) such that every vertex of \(S\) reaches some vertex of \(T\) in \((V,B)\), and every vertex of \(T\) is reachable from some vertex of \(S\). Its minimum size is \[\tau(D;S,T)=\min\{|B|:B\subseteq A\text{ is an }S\text{–}T\text{ bibranching}\}.\] Equivalently, feasible incidence vectors satisfy \(x(\delta^+(X))\ge1\) for every nonempty \(X\subseteq S\) and \(x(\delta^-(Y))\ge1\) for every nonempty \(Y\subseteq T\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A minimum-size bibranching uses the fewest arcs while connecting every S vertex toward T and every T vertex from S.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\tau(D;S,T)=\min\{\mathbf1^\top x:x\in\{0,1\}^A,\ x(\delta^+(X))\ge1,\ x(\delta^-(Y))\ge1\}.\)

knowledge_statements.title: Bifurcation Duality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cut-packing dual associated with the weighted bibranching covering program.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the shortest-bibranching program on \(V=S\mathbin{\dot\cup}T\), assign \(p_X\ge0\) to each nonempty \(X\subseteq S\) and \(q_Y\ge0\) to each nonempty \(Y\subseteq T\). An integral or combinatorial interpretation of an optimal dual support is called a bifurcation.

knowledge_statements.title: Disjoint R–S Biconnectors
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Arc-disjoint packing characterized by two families of separating cuts.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D=(V,A)\) and let \(R,S\subseteq V\) be disjoint and nonempty. There exist \(k\) pairwise arc-disjoint \(R\)–\(S\) biconnectors if and only if \(|\delta^+(X)|\ge k\) for every \(X\subseteq V\) with \(X\cap R\ne\varnothing\) and \(X\cap S=\varnothing\), and \(|\delta^-(X)|\ge k\) for every \(X\subseteq V\) with \(X\cap S\ne\varnothing\) and \(X\cap R=\varnothing\). Consequently, the maximum packing number is the minimum cardinality among these two classes of directed separating cuts.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The maximum number of arc-disjoint R–S biconnectors equals the smallest outgoing or incoming cut separating one prescribed side from the other.

e\varnothing,\ X\cap S=\varnothing,\ Y\cap S
e\varnothing,\ Y\cap R=\varnothing igr\}.\)

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let G=(V,E), where V=R\mathbin{\dot\cup}S. knowledge_statements.title: Biforest Coverings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Set-cover formulation for covering arcs by directed biforests.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D=(V,A)\) and let \(\mathcal F_{R,S}(D)\subseteq2^A\) be its source-defined family of \(R\)–\(S\) biforests. A biforest covering is a finite indexed family \((F_i)_{i=1}^m\) with \(F_i\in\mathcal F_{R,S}(D)\) and \(A\subseteq\bigcup_{i=1}^mF_i\). Its covering number is \[\chi_{\mathrm{bf}}(D;R,S)=\min\left\{m:A\subseteq\bigcup_{i=1}^mF_i,\ F_i\in\mathcal F_{R,S}(D)\right\}.\] If no such family exists, the value is \(+\infty\). The exact structural axioms for the intended biforest family require source confirmation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A biforest covering is a collection of R–S biforests whose union contains every arc; its covering number is the smallest collection size.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\chi_{\mathrm{bf}}(D;R,S)=\min\{m:A\subseteq\bigcup_{i=1}^mF_i,\ F_i\in\mathcal F_{R,S}(D)\}.\)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Tutte–Nash-Williams Tree-Packing Criterion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Partition-cut characterization of the existence of edge-disjoint spanning trees.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $G$ be an undirected graph and let $k\ge 1$. Then $G$ contains $k$ pairwise edge-disjoint spanning trees if and only if, for every partition $V(G)=X_1\mathbin{\dot\cup}\cdots\mathbin{\dot\cup}X_p$ into nonempty sets, $|\delta(X_1,\ldots,X_p)|\ge k(p-1)$.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: G\text{ contains }k\text{ pairwise edge-disjoint spanning trees}\iff \forall(X_1,\ldots,X_p),\ |\delta(X_1,\ldots,X_p)|\ge k(p-1)

knowledge_statements.title: Partition Connectivity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Partition inequality governing edge-disjoint spanning-tree packings.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite undirected multigraph and let \(k\in\mathbb Z_+\). For a partition \(\mathcal P\) of \(V\), let \(e_G(\mathcal P)\) be the number of edges whose endpoints lie in distinct blocks. The graph is \(k\)-partition-connected when \[e_G(\mathcal P)\ge k\bigl(|\mathcal P|-1\bigr)\] for every partition \(\mathcal P\) of \(V\). By the Tutte–Nash-Williams theorem, this condition is equivalent to the existence of \(k\) pairwise edge-disjoint spanning trees in \(G\). Parallel edges are counted with multiplicity; loops never cross a partition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A graph is k-partition-connected when every vertex partition has at least k times one fewer crossing edges; equivalently, it packs k edge-disjoint spanning trees.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G\text{ contains }k\text{ edge-disjoint spanning trees}\iff e_G(\mathcal P)\ge k(|\mathcal P|-1)\) for every partition \(\mathcal P\).

notation.meaning: a partition of the vertex set
number of edges joining distinct partition blocks

knowledge_statements.title: Tight Partition Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equality partitions certifying saturation of the tree-packing bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite \(k\)-partition-connected multigraph, and let \(T_1,\ldots,T_k\) be pairwise edge-disjoint spanning trees. A partition \(\mathcal P\) of \(V\) is tight when \[e_G(\mathcal P)=k\bigl(|\mathcal P|-1\bigr).\] For every tight partition \(\mathcal P\), each packed tree satisfies \[|E(T_i)\cap\delta(\mathcal P)|=|\mathcal P|-1\qquad(i=1,\ldots,k),\] and every edge in \(\delta(\mathcal P)\) belongs to exactly one of the packed trees. Thus the tight partition certifies saturation of the partition bound by the packing.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A tight partition meets the tree-packing inequality with equality and certifies that every packed tree uses exactly one fewer crossing edges than the number of partition blocks, with all crossing edges saturated by the packing.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(e_G(\mathcal P)=k(|\mathcal P|-1)\Rightarrow |E(T_i)\cap\delta(\mathcal P)|=|\mathcal P|-1\) for every \(i\), and \(\delta(\mathcal P)\subseteq\bigcup_{i=1}^kE(T_i)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A capacitated packing of size \(k\) is a multiset of spanning trees \(T_1,\ldots,T_k\) such that every edge \(e\) occurs in at most \(c(e)\) members. Such a packing exists exactly when, for every partition \(\mathcal P\) of \(V\),
\[c(\delta_G(\mathcal P))\ge k(|\mathcal P|-1).\]
Hence the maximum feasible integer value equals
\[\tau_c(G)=\min_{\mathcal P:\,|\mathcal P|\ge2}\left\lfloor\frac{c(\delta_G(\mathcal P))}{|\mathcal P|-1}\right\rfloor.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Integral edge capacities support k spanning trees exactly when every vertex partition has capacity at least k times its block count minus one.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The fractional tree-packing value is
\[\max\left\{\sum_{T\in\mathcal T(G)}x_T:x_T\ge0,\ \sum_{T\ni e}x_T\le c(e)\ \text{for every }e\in E\right\}.\]
Its linear-programming dual is
\[\min\left\{\sum_{e\in E}c(e)y_e:y_e\ge0,\ \sum_{e\in T}y_e\ge1\ \text{for every }T\in\mathcal T(G)\right\}.\]
Both optima equal
\[\min_{\mathcal P:\,|\mathcal P|\ge2}\frac{c(\delta_G(\mathcal P))}{|\mathcal P|-1}.\]

children.top_down_role: Weighted optimization over unions of multiple spanning trees.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite connected undirected graph.
\(w:E\to\mathbb R\) assigns an edge weight and \(k\in\mathbb Z_{\ge1}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The optimum is \(\displaystyle\min\{\sum_{e\in U}w(e):U=T_1\dot\cup\cdots\dot\cup T_k,\ T_i\text{ spanning trees}\}\), when the feasible family is nonempty.

notation.meaning: Union of the packed spanning trees
Total weight of an edge set

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses edge-disjoint trees and charges each selected edge once.

source_refs.locator: Section 6.4. Packing Spanning Trees and Arborescences p. 147

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A feasible union of \(k\) spanning trees is an edge set \(U\subseteq E\) admitting a disjoint decomposition
\[U=T_1\mathbin{\dot\cup}\cdots\mathbin{\dot\cup}T_k,\]
where every \(T_i\) is a spanning tree of \(G\). The minimum-weight-union problem minimizes \(w(U)=\sum_{e\in U}w(e)\) over all such decompositions. Feasibility is equivalent to
\[|\delta_G(\mathcal P)|\ge k(|\mathcal P|-1)\]
for every partition \(\mathcal P\) of \(V\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose k edge-disjoint spanning trees and minimize the total weight of their union; partition inequalities characterize feasibility.
knowledge_statements.title: Minimum-Weight Unions of Spanning Trees

source_witnesses.locator: Section 6.4. Packing Spanning Trees and Arborescences p. 147

children.title: Spanning-Forest Packing
children.top_down_role: Packing regimes centered on undirected spanning forests.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A packing is a tuple \((F_1,\ldots,F_k)\) satisfying \(F_i\cap F_j=\varnothing\), acyclicity of every \(F_i\), and \(|F_i|=r_i\).

notation.meaning: The ith spanning forest edge set
Required rank or edge count of the ith forest

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Spanning means all vertices are retained; isolated vertices are permitted.

source_refs.locator: 10.5 Packing trees and forests p. 363

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A spanning-forest packing with rank profile \((r_1,\ldots,r_k)\) is a tuple of pairwise edge-disjoint sets \((F_1,\ldots,F_k)\) such that each graph \((V,F_i)\) is acyclic and \(|F_i|=r_i\). Since all vertices are retained, \((V,F_i)\) has exactly \(|V|-r_i\) connected components, including isolated vertices. The unprofiled version asks for forests satisfying prescribed lower bounds or maximizing \(\sum_{i=1}^k|F_i|\) subject to edge-disjointness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A spanning-forest packing consists of edge-disjoint acyclic spanning subgraphs, optionally with prescribed edge counts or component counts.
knowledge_statements.title: Spanning-Forest Packing

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Maximum Cardinality of a Union of k Forests
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Here \(\delta(\mathcal P)\) is the set of edges joining distinct classes of \(\mathcal P\), and each forest is an edge subset of \(G\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,E)\) be an undirected graph and \(k\in\mathbb Z_+\). Then
\[
\max_{F_1,\ldots,F_k\text{ forests in }G}\left|\bigcup_{i=1}^k F_i\right|=\min_{\mathcal P}\left\{|\delta(\mathcal P)|+k(|V|-|\mathcal P|)\right\},
\]
where the minimum ranges over all partitions \(\mathcal P\) of \(V\) into nonempty classes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For an undirected graph and a positive integer k, the maximum number of edges in a union of k forests equals the minimum, over all partitions of the vertex set into nonempty classes, of the number of crossing edges plus k times the number of vertices minus the number of classes.
assumptions_latex: \mathcal P\text{ ranges over partitions of }V\text{ into nonempty classes}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \max_{F_1,\ldots,F_k\text{ forests in }G}\left|\bigcup_{i=1}^kF_i\right|=\min_{\mathcal P}\bigl(|\delta(\mathcal P)|+k(|V|-|\mathcal P|)\bigr)

children.title: Tree–Forest Packing Relations
children.top_down_role: Structural transitions between tree packings and forest packings.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite undirected graph with \(|V|=n\).
\(F_1,\ldots,F_k\subseteq E\) are pairwise edge-disjoint spanning forests.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The forests are spanning trees exactly when \(|F_i|=n-1\) for every \(i\).

notation.meaning: Number of connected components of the ith spanning forest

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relates forest rank deficits to connectivity and tree packings.

source_refs.locator: 10.5 Packing trees and forests p. 363

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every spanning forest \((V,F_i)\), its component count satisfies \[q_i=n-|F_i|.\] Thus \(F_i\) is a spanning tree if and only if \(|F_i|=n-1\), equivalently \(q_i=1\). A packing of \(k\) spanning forests is a packing of \(k\) spanning trees if and only if \[\sum_{i=1}^k|F_i|=k(n-1).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A packed spanning forest is a tree precisely when it has n minus one edges; a forest packing is a tree packing precisely when its total size is k times n minus one.
knowledge_statements.title: Tree–Forest Packing Relations

children.title: Nash-Williams Arboricity Theorem Family
children.top_down_role: Density-based characterization of forest covers.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite loopless undirected multigraph with at least one edge.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\displaystyle a(G)=\max_{H\subseteq G,\,|V(H)|\ge2}\left\lceil\frac{|E(H)|}{|V(H)|-1}\right\rceil\).

notation.meaning: Minimum number of forests whose edge sets cover E
A nontrivial subgraph of G

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite loopless multigraph form of the Nash-Williams arboricity theorem.

source_refs.locator: 10.5 Packing trees and forests p. 363

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The arboricity \(a(G)\), defined as the least \(k\) for which \(E\) is the union of \(k\) forests, satisfies
\[a(G)=\max_{H\subseteq G,\,|V(H)|\ge2}\left\lceil\frac{|E(H)|}{|V(H)|-1}\right\rceil.\]
Equivalently, \(E\) decomposes into \(k\) forests if and only if every subgraph \(H\) with at least two vertices obeys
\[|E(H)|\le k(|V(H)|-1).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The arboricity equals the largest rounded-up edge density using vertices minus one, taken over all nontrivial subgraphs.
knowledge_statements.title: Nash-Williams Arboricity Theorem Family

children.title: Pseudoforest-Orientation Correspondence

children.title: Pseudoforest Decompositions
children.top_down_role: Edge-set decompositions into pseudoforest components.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite loopless undirected multigraph with at least one edge.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(E\) decomposes into \(k\) pseudoforests if and only if \(|E(H)|\le k|V(H)|\) for every nonempty subgraph \(H\subseteq G\).

notation.meaning: Minimum number of pseudoforests partitioning E
A subgraph of G containing at least one edge

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pseudoforests have at most one cycle in each connected component.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A pseudoforest is a graph in which every connected component contains at most one cycle. The edge set \(E\) can be partitioned into \(k\) pseudoforests if and only if every nonempty subgraph \(H\subseteq G\) satisfies
\[|E(H)|\le k|V(H)|.\]
Consequently, the pseudoarboricity is
\[p(G)=\max_{H\subseteq G,\,|E(H)|>0}\left\lceil\frac{|E(H)|}{|V(H)|}\right\rceil.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Edges split into k pseudoforests exactly when every nonempty subgraph has at most k times as many edges as vertices.
knowledge_statements.title: Pseudoforest Decompositions

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The pseudoforest decomposition criterion is plausible and standard, but the record supplies no source reference or inspectable locator. Authoritative sourcing is required before the theorem can enter candidate-review knowledge.

children.title: Bounded-Outdegree Orientations
children.top_down_role: Orientation counterparts governed by local outdegree limits.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite loopless undirected multigraph.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An orientation with \(d_D^+(v)\le k\) for every vertex exists exactly when \(|E(X)|\le k|X|\) for every \(X\subseteq V\).

notation.meaning: Outdegree of v in orientation D
Edges having both endpoints in X

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniform outdegree bound; parallel edges are allowed and loops are excluded.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
There exists an orientation \(D\) of every edge of \(G\) such that
\[d_D^+(v)\le k\qquad\text{for every }v\in V\]
if and only if
\[|E(X)|\le k|X|\qquad\text{for every }X\subseteq V.\]
The necessity follows by charging each edge induced by \(X\) to its tail in \(X\); the displayed inequalities constitute the complete feasibility predicate for the bounded-outdegree orientation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A graph admits an orientation of maximum outdegree k exactly when every vertex subset induces at most k times its size edges.
knowledge_statements.title: Bounded-Outdegree Orientations

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The bounded-outdegree orientation criterion is standard and fits the condition leaf, but no source or locator is supplied. The statement also contains a necessity argument that must be removed when a sourced replacement is prepared.

knowledge_statements.title: Decomposition–Orientation Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite loopless multigraph version of the pseudoforest decomposition correspondence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite loopless undirected multigraph and let \(k\ge 1\). Then \(E\) can be partitioned into \(k\) pseudoforests if and only if the edges of \(G\) admit an orientation \(D\) satisfying \(d_D^+(v)\le k\) for every \(v\in V\). Here a pseudoforest is a graph in which every connected component contains at most one cycle.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite multigraph decomposes into k pseudoforests exactly when its edges can be oriented with every vertex having outdegree at most k.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(E\text{ partitions into }k\text{ pseudoforests}\iff \exists D\;\forall v\in V,\ d_D^+(v)\le k.\)

notation.meaning: Outdegree of vertex v in orientation D.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cut characterization for arc-disjoint spanning arborescences whose prescribed roots may differ.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D=(V,A)\) be a digraph and let \(r_1,\ldots,r_k\in V\). There exist pairwise arc-disjoint arborescences \(B_1,\ldots,B_k\), where \(B_i\) has root \(r_i\), if and only if \[d^{\mathrm{in}}(U)\geq |\{i:r_i\notin U\}|\] for every nonempty \(U\subseteq V\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Equivalent Characterizations of Packing Rooted Arborescences
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalence among rooted-arborescence packing, directed cut conditions, local path packings, and a spanning-tree representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D=(V,A)\) be a digraph, let \(r\in V\), and let \(k\in\mathbb Z_+\). The following are equivalent: (i) there exist \(k\) pairwise arc-disjoint \(r\)-arborescences; (ii) \(d^{\mathrm{in}}(U)\geq k\) for every nonempty \(U\subseteq V\setminus\{r\}\); (iii) for each \(s\neq r\), there exist \(k\) arc-disjoint directed \(r\)-\(s\) paths in \(D\); (iv) there exist \(k\) edge-disjoint spanning trees in the underlying undirected graph such that, for each \(s\neq r\), exactly \(k\) arcs entering \(s\) are covered by these trees.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For each positive integer k, packing k arc-disjoint r-arborescences is equivalent to the k-entry cut condition, to having k arc-disjoint paths from r to every other vertex, and to the stated edge-disjoint spanning-tree representation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{(i)}\Longleftrightarrow\text{(ii)}\Longleftrightarrow\text{(iii)}\Longleftrightarrow\text{(iv)}
